expert_analysis:
Gibbs is the only running back to average at least 21 PPR points per game in each of the last two seasons, combining elite rushing efficiency, double-digit touchdown production and over 500 receiving yards. The departure of David Montgomery removes the main factor that had previously capped his goal-line ceiling.

Detroit’s offensive line is the primary concern after dropping from second to 13th in PFF run-blocking grade last season. Two more starters were replaced this offseason, adding further uncertainty to an area central to Gibbs’ production. New offensive coordinator Drew Petzing has shown a willingness to feature a lead back heavily, so a dramatic shift in usage is unlikely.

The same talented supporting cast that creates slight competition for touches also helps Detroit remain one of the league's best offenses. The other elite running backs at a similar ADP carry comparable or greater uncertainty, which keeps Gibbs at the top of the position.

Robinson has finished among the top-three fantasy running backs in each of the last two seasons, combining over 1,400 rushing yards and at least 60 receptions per year. The replacement of Tyler Allgeier with Brian Robinson Jr. at backup is a lateral move at worst for his goal-line outlook.

Kevin Stefanski's history of featuring a lead back heavily when the personnel warrants it is an encouraging sign, as is his track record of prioritizing the running back position going back to his time with Dalvin Cook in Minnesota.

The Atlanta offensive line is the primary concern, with Jake Matthews posting a career-low PFF run-blocking grade and Kaleb McGary‘s retirement forcing Atlanta to sign Jawaan Taylor, who profiles more as a pass protector than a run blocker. Robinson is competing with Jahmyr Gibbs for the top running back spot, with Gibbs holding a slight edge due to Detroit's offensive track record and fewer questions up front.

Nacua has been the most productive wide receiver in the NFL over the past two seasons with a 96.3 PFF receiving grade that leads the position comfortably. He has backed that up with elite performances against top defenses, including accruing 19 receptions for 300 yards and two touchdowns across two games against Seattle last season.

The Rams maintained every significant offensive piece outside of Rob Havenstein‘s retirement and own the highest PFF team grade in the league, but an upgraded defense could reduce passing volume enough to keep Nacua from reaching his ceiling as the overall WR1.

Matthew Stafford turns 38 before the season after an MVP campaign, making at least some regression in his efficiency metrics a reasonable expectation. The long-term dynasty outlook adds another variable with first-round pick Ty Simpson waiting in the wings, though Nacua's elite production makes him a locked-in early first-round pick in redraft regardless.

McCaffrey led all running backs in fantasy points last season, getting there with modest rushing production and elite, wide receiver-level work in the passing game. But the concerns are mounting: a 3.

9 yards-per-carry average, fewer explosive runs, declining top-end speed on tracking data and a rebuilt 49ers receiving corps that could cut into the target volume that drove his value.

Combined with his age and a long injury history, that profile moves McCaffrey out of the top tier of backs, even though the overall RB1 upside is still there if everything breaks right. He lands as a mid-first-round redraft pick.

Chase reached a career-high 90.1 PFF receiving grade this past season, closing the gap between himself and the elite receivers thanks to Joe Burrow, whose 94.2 PFF passing grade over the past two seasons is notably higher than that of any other quarterback.

No wide receiver dominates a favorable matchup as well as Chase, who has put together five games with double-digit receptions for 160 or more yards and at least one touchdown over the past two years, compared to nine for the rest of the league combined.

The key members of the Bengals who have helped Chase will remain in place, with 20 of the 22 players who logged at least 25 offensive snaps last season still on the roster. The primary reason he isn't ranked as the top receiver in redraft is his performance in tough showdowns. Chase averaged just 33 yards across three games against top-eight defenses in preventing fantasy points to wide receivers.

Taylor was one of fantasy's most productive backs through the first 12 weeks of 2025, averaging 25.7 PPR points per game before fading to 13.3 over the final third as his boom-or-bust rushing style cooled off. His 71.

4 PFF grade across the past two seasons sits below the other backs drafted this early, but Taylor stays a top-five option because the Colts have again declined to invest behind him, leaving him with one of the league's heaviest workloads.

The risks are a long injury history and an uncertain quarterback picture with Daniel Jones coming back from injury. Taylor is a deserving first-round pick, just not a sure thing.

Smith-Njigba was incredibly consistent in 2025, finishing with at least 90 receiving yards in all but two games. He’s also the youngest of the early first-round wide receiver options, making further improvement more likely than with the others.

The reason Smith-Njigba ranks a little lower in redraft is that the Seahawks underwent more significant changes this offseason, most notably losing offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak to the Las Vegas Raiders’ head coaching job and replacing him with former 49ers tight ends coach Brian Fleury.

The reigning Offensive Player of the Year should have consistency at quarterback with Sam Darnold, who ranks among the top-10 quarterbacks in PFF grade over the last two seasons, though Darnold hasn't been as good as Burrow or Stafford. No one is going to come close to taking Smith-Njigba's spot as the top receiving weapon in the offense, but he remains on top in dynasty rankings thanks to his age, and the situation for each wide receiver is temporary.

Allen has been a top-three fantasy quarterback in each of the past six seasons, combining elite passing consistency with rushing production that includes 12 or more touchdowns on the ground in each of the past three years.

What separates him historically is the balance between his skill sets, as he is a more polished passer than most elite rushing quarterbacks and a more dangerous runner than most high-end pocket passers. The only real concern is age, as elite rushing production tends to decline earlier than passing ability, and Allen turned 30 before the season starts.

Buffalo's addition of DJ Moore should push his passing volume back up after a down year in 2025, giving him a realistic path to an even bigger season and making him the top fantasy quarterback option by a clear margin in redraft.

Hurts has finished among the top eight fantasy quarterbacks in each of the past five seasons, a consistency matched only by Josh Allen, but 2025 was a down year across the board with career lows in yards per attempt and rushing output.

The concerns around Patrick Mahomes‘ ACL recovery, Lamar Jackson‘s aging supporting cast and the situation around Rashee Rice in Kansas City all work in Hurts' favor as one of the safer options at the position. Philadelphia replaced A.J. Brown with Makai Lemon, Dontayvion Wicks and Hollywood Brown.

While the receiver room took a step back on paper, the Eagles should still field a top-10 offense with new coordinator Sean Mannion committed to keeping Hurts' rushing ability central to the scheme. A bounce-back season in both his efficiency metrics and rushing production would make him a top-three fantasy quarterback, and the surrounding circumstances give him a reasonable path to get there.

Maye delivered one of the best sophomore seasons by a quarterback in the past two decades, ranking second in total fantasy points and third in points per game. The additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs give him a significantly stronger supporting cast heading into 2026. Maye’s 8.9 yards per attempt led the league, and his touchdown and interception rates both point toward at least some regression.

On top of that, his 409 rushing yards fell short of the 500-yard threshold that most top-three fantasy quarterbacks have cleared in recent seasons. Maye remains the top dynasty quarterback asset and a strong redraft option, though Josh Allen is the safer pick in redraft given his longer track record of elite production.

The schedule-strength concerns from 2025 are somewhat overstated given that Maye averaged 21.9 fantasy points per game against top-eight defenses, but regression in efficiency metrics is a real possibility that keeps him just below Allen in redraft tiers.

Jackson is the only quarterback to ever average 25 fantasy points per game in multiple seasons and has the highest ceiling of any quarterback in the top five, but his rushing attempts have declined every season since 2021 and dropped to just 5.2 per game in 2025.

The Ravens overhauled their entire coaching staff, with first-time play-caller Declan Doyle taking over as offensive coordinator after a season in Chicago — where he held the title but did not call plays — and the roster lost several key offensive pieces in free agency while leaning on a core of players past their prime.

Some rebound in Jackson's rushing production is reasonable to expect, and his passing efficiency has remained consistently strong. But the combination of declining mobility, a first-year play-caller and significant roster turnover makes him a boom-or-bust option rather than a safe top-five quarterback. His dynasty value remains elite given his track record, but in redraft he carries more risk than Allen, Maye or Hurts at a similar ADP.

Jefferson was a top-five fantasy wide receiver in points per game each season from 2021 to 2024. That streak ended in 2025 when he finished 30th, largely because his catchable target rate dropped nearly 10% and his end zone catchable target rate fell from 50% to 25% with Carson Wentz and J.J.

McCarthy under center. The Vikings addressed the quarterback situation by signing Kyler Murray, the best available option. Murray has supported elite fantasy receivers before, including DeAndre Hopkins as a top-five receiver in 2020 and Trey McBride‘s TE2 season in 2024.

There is always some risk with a new quarterback, but Murray represents a significant upgrade over what Jefferson dealt with last season. This change should be enough to return Jefferson to the top-five fantasy wide receivers.

St. Brown has finished fourth, fifth and fourth in fantasy points per game among wide receivers over the last three seasons while posting a PFF receiving grade between 90.0 and 91.3 in each of the last four, making him the safest wide receiver available in fantasy drafts.

There isn't much reason to expect a significant change in either direction: He accumulates plus-0.5-graded receptions at a high rate but doesn't make big plays at nearly the rate of the top-three receivers on this list, and the Lions have enough weapons that they don't need to lean on him more heavily.

The main worry is new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, who didn't prioritize slot receivers in Arizona, and Jameson Williams‘ continued development could eat into St. Brown's role. Those were the same issues last season, though, and they had no impact on his production.

Achane is one of the most talented running backs in the league and the clear focal point of Miami's offense, which makes him a safe top-10 option.

But the ecosystem around him works against a higher finish: The Dolphins' run-blocking has ranked among the worst in the league, the offense has struggled to score and an offseason of departures raises the risk that it takes another step back.

With Achane’s volume already historic for his size and little room to grow, he profiles as a strong starter but an unlikely bet to crack the very top backs.

Cook finished 11th among running backs in points per game in 2024 on the back of 16 rushing touchdowns, and the expected touchdown regression pushed his draft cost down. But 2025 made the case that he can keep producing: his carries jumped from 12.

9 to 19.1 a game without cutting into his receiving work, he stayed efficient at 5.3 yards per carry and Buffalo's offensive line improved to sixth in PFF run-blocking grade.

The offseason did little to change Cook’s outlook, with the backfield intact and no clear move toward a pass-heavier attack. He's well-positioned for similar value in 2026, with a modestly lighter workload the main risk.

Daniels was a top-five fantasy quarterback as a rookie on the strength of his rushing, posting 148 carries for 891 yards and six touchdowns, numbers no other quarterback came close to matching. But a knee sprain, hamstring strain and dislocated elbow limited him to just one fully healthy game in 2025.

Daniels’ rushing ability gives him a realistic shot at finishing as the top fantasy quarterback in 2026 if he stays healthy, and there is enough cushion in his rushing volume that he does not need to fully replicate his rookie output to remain elite.

The concern is a significant supporting cast overhaul, with five of the six Commanders who had 40 or more receptions over the past two seasons now off the roster, plus first-time play-caller David Blough stepping in as offensive coordinator. The combination of injury history, roster turnover and an unproven coordinator makes Daniels a high-upside, high-variance option rather than a safe top-three quarterback.

Lamb has reached 1,000 yards in five straight seasons and started 2025 as well as anyone, with 10 consecutive games of at least 66 receiving yards. Yet he finished just 10th in fantasy points per game, largely because he was held to three touchdowns against a career average of seven.

Positive touchdown regression alone should push him back into the top-five conversation, especially in one of the league's most stable offenses. The Cowboys retained both their head coach and offensive coordinator, Dak Prescott returns at quarterback and each of the top 11 players by offensive snaps from last season remains on the roster.

George Pickens‘ presence will make it difficult to replicate Lamb’s 2023 fantasy heights, but it also means defenses can't focus solely on Lamb. He is a very safe bet for another top-10 finish if healthy.

London is one of the league's elite receivers, joining Puka Nacua and Amon-Ra St. Brown as the only wide receivers with an 89.0-plus PFF receiving grade in each of the past two seasons. On top of that, London’s fantasy points per game jumped from 15.0 in 2024 to 16.8 in 2025, good for seventh among wideouts.

He benefits from limited competition for targets, with the players who ate into his volume last season all having departed, and Bijan Robinson and Kyle Pitts remaining as his only significant competition. The primary problem is the quarterback situation, with Michael Penix Jr. still rehabbing a torn ACL and Tua Tagovailoa competing for the starting job, though Tagovailoa has supported elite fantasy receivers before.

The secondary concern is new head coach Kevin Stefanski, whose teams haven't produced a top-15 fantasy wide receiver in points per game across seven seasons as a head coach or coordinator. Yet London has been more consistently excellent than any receiver Stefanski has previously coached.

Burrow finished as the QB3 in 2024 and ranked third in fantasy points per game from his return in Week 13 through Week 18 last season after an early injury cut his year short. Nearly every piece around him returns in 2026 with Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and the coaching staff all locked in long-term.

Burrow does not rely on rushing production like most top fantasy quarterbacks, instead deriving his value from elite passing efficiency and one of the league's most pass-heavy offenses, a product in part of Cincinnati's defense ranking among the seven worst in points allowed in each of the last two seasons.

The Bengals made a significant investment to fix that, trading the 10th overall pick for Dexter Lawrence and adding Bryan Cook and Boye Mafe in free agency, which could reduce the negative game scripts that have driven Burrow's volume. If the defense improves enough to change how Cincinnati manages games, Burrow’s passing volume could dip, but his injury history is the bigger concern given he has missed at least six games in three of his six NFL seasons.

Jeanty was selected sixth overall in the 2025 NFL Draft, a draft slot that typically supports immediate top-10 fantasy production, but several factors outside of his control limited his rookie output. Despite playing behind one of the worst offensive lines in the NFL, he forced 61 missed tackles on the ground, ranking fifth among running backs.

Jeanty also placed fourth in PFF rushing grade (92.3) on carries with positive yards before contact, suggesting significant upside in an improved environment. The Raiders addressed that situation aggressively this offseason, hiring Klint Kubiak as head coach, drafting quarterback Fernando Mendoza first overall and signing elite center Tyler Linderbaum.

One concern is Kubiak's tendency to deploy a true two-back system, with fourth-round rookie Mike Washington Jr. (223 pounds) threatening to siphon goal-line work from Jeanty (208) the same way Zach Charbonnet did from Kenneth Walker III in Seattle. A bigger concern is Jeanty suffered a sprained ankle on Aug. 23. It's unclear the extent of the sprain, and if he will be ready to go for Week 1 or if he will miss some time.

Brown has finished top 10 among running backs in fantasy points per game in each of the last two years. The setup in Cincinnati remains consistent, with Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins keeping defenses from loading the box.

On top of that, Brown ranks among the top running backs in both first-read and checkdown targets. The only real concern is Burrow's health, but when he was fully healthy down the stretch last season, Brown averaged 22.

3 PPR points per game without even breaking a long run. That suggests even more upside if the Cincinnati offense fully clicks.

Herbert has been a reliable fantasy quarterback since he entered the league, and his outlook is even better this year with a new offensive coordinator, an improving young supporting cast and a healthier offensive line.

The biggest lift to his ceiling is his rushing, which jumped to 498 yards last season, second-most among quarterbacks. That gives Herbert overall QB1 upside, with the main caveat a recurring pattern of injuries to his skill players derailing promising seasons.

In single-quarterback leagues, Herbert is worth waiting on rather than reaching for an early quarterback, ideally paired with a second option for tough matchups.

Purdy has finished among the top 12 quarterbacks in each of his three seasons as a starter, doing it both with a loaded supporting cast and through stretches of heavy injuries. His 91.1 offensive grade ranks sixth at the position over that span.

Purdy is going outside the top 12 despite play that warrants a spot inside it, and San Francisco's offseason additions of Mike Evans and Christian Kirk should give him his best receiving group in years.

The main risk is how many of his key weapons are aging veterans, since a decline from one or more could drag down the whole offense. On balance, Purdy is an undervalued quarterback and a strong reason to feel comfortable waiting at the position.

Lawrence broke out as a fantasy asset in 2025 under new head coach Liam Coen, finishing sixth among quarterbacks in points per game while setting career highs in rushing.

Much of that production came from his rapport with Parker Washington, Jakobi Meyers and Brenton Strange as much as his higher-profile targets, and having his full receiving group healthy at once should sustain it.

Even with some expected touchdown regression, Lawrence’s outlook is similar to last season, which makes his current ADP outside the top 10 a strong value.

Walker has been one of the most efficient running backs in the NFL over the past three seasons, ranking second in PFF overall grade (93.

2), but a crowded backfield in Seattle limited his fantasy value by splitting goal-line work and passing game opportunities with Zach Charbonnet. With Isiah Pacheco gone and Kareem Hunt unsigned, the Chiefs present a much cleaner path.

While Kansas City's pass-heavy tendencies cap Walker’s rushing ceiling, the team's history of targeting running backs and Walker's own receiving ability give him a realistic shot at a top-five finish if his role in the passing game expands.

Prescott has been the Cowboys' starter for a decade and finished eighth in fantasy points per game last season behind one of the league's best supporting casts, with CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, a strong offensive line and a pass-friendly staff all returning.

He offers little as a runner, and a step back is reasonable now that an overhauled defense should keep Dallas from trailing and throwing as often late in games.

Prescott’s production swings with the strength of his opponent, ranging from QB8 against weak defenses to QB16 against top-10 units. Prescott is a fine single-quarterback option who is best paired with a second quarterback you can stream by matchup.

Williams was a non-factor as a rookie, but the additions of Ben Johnson, Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland helped him jump to 19.0 fantasy points per game last season, eighth-most among quarterbacks. He wasn't consistent on a play-by-play basis, as his 57.

0% accuracy ranked second-worst among qualifying passers, but volume and a 27-to-9 touchdown-to-interception ratio carried his fantasy value. Williams’ 77 carries for 383 yards also gave him a useful rushing floor.

Some regression is possible given the accuracy concerns. But a second year in Johnson's system and a young receiving corps that finished strong both point toward growth, making Williams a fantasy starter this season and one of the top dynasty options at the position.

Murray was a steady top-12 fantasy quarterback for five seasons before injury wrecked his 2025 and a healthy-but-unproductive 2024 raised real questions, but he's landing in a Kevin O'Connell offense that has produced fantasy-relevant quarterbacks in nearly every season regardless of who's behind center.

An improving offensive line that battled injuries up front last year should help. Pairing with Justin Jefferson, who grades out even better than DeAndre Hopkins did during Murray's best Arizona stretch, gives him a real path back to weekly fantasy relevance.

If Murray and the Minnesota offense both bounce back, he profiles as a consistent single-quarterback starter.

Mahomes bounced back to a top-two fantasy finish last season, but the rebound was driven almost entirely by a spike in rushing rather than his passing, which has quietly declined for years.

Even with a Week 1 return expected, that matters because a torn ACL and LCL makes it unlikely he runs as much this season, removing the exact thing that fueled his 2025 value.

Add in an aging Travis Kelce, a possible Rashee Rice suspension and a down year from Xavier Worthy, and there's real risk, though the return of coordinator Eric Bieniemy from Mahomes’ peak years offers upside. He's worth drafting in single-quarterback leagues but should be paired with a second option to stream by matchup.

Nix has been a top-10 fantasy quarterback in each of his two pro seasons, but his production has outrun his PFF passing grade — propped up by elite volume, a top pass-blocking line, a strong defense and his own rushing.

Several of those supports could soften this year: A healthy backfield led by J.K. Dobbins could pull rushing volume from Nix, especially with a good defense inviting run-heavy game scripts, and an ankle injury may curb his own runs.

The addition of Jaylen Waddle should help Nix as a passer, so he could look better while producing less for fantasy. Nix’s ADP has rightly dipped, and he profiles as a quarterback to pair with another in single-quarterback leagues.

Dart averaged 20.5 fantasy points per start as a rookie, ranking seventh among quarterbacks. His rushing ability was the primary driver, as his 86 attempts and nine touchdowns on the ground carried his fantasy value despite modest passing efficiency.

The supporting cast around him is dramatically improved heading into 2026, with Malik Nabers ideally returning from a torn ACL, the additions of Darnell Mooney, Calvin Austin III and Isaiah Likely and the 10th overall pick spent on offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa.

A healthy Nabers is likely the key variable separating Dart from the top tier of fantasy quarterbacks, as the rest of the receiver upgrades alone may not be enough to push him there. Concussion questions are the other limiting factor, as he missed two games and underwent multiple evaluations last season, keeping him just outside the top tier despite the upside.

Brown was ranked the top wide receiver entering 2025 but posted a relative dip in production, with speculation that situational frustration rather than physical decline was the cause, as Philadelphia's dominant rushing attack repeatedly rendered him a spectator in lopsided wins.

He was traded to New England, where he reunited with head coach Mike Vrabel and is the clear top skill player on the roster. The fit looks promising on paper: Brown's 12.8 average depth of target over the last three seasons is the highest among the top-10 wide receivers by PFF grade, and Drake Maye ranked fourth among quarterbacks on passes of 13 or more yards at 49.

7%, compared to Jalen Hurts‘ third-lowest rate of 36.8% among the top 30. If the 2025 decline was situational, Brown has the ceiling for an elite fantasy campaign; if it marked the beginning of a broader downturn, managers could be in for a disappointing year.

Stafford is coming off an MVP season and the fourth-most fantasy points per game, but his production leaned heavily on a career-best touchdown rate and career-low interception rate that are strong regression candidates.

If his touchdown rate falls even to his 2023 level, his scoring will drop enough to land him around QB18. Add in his age, 38, and a Rams defense that added talent and is expected to improve — likely cutting pass volume and inviting run-heavy fourth quarters — and the outlook is cautious.

Stafford is a matchup-based option who shouldn't be drafted as a starter in single-quarterback leagues, and he ranks even lower in dynasty.

Goff has been remarkably durable and productive in raw passing terms, leading all quarterbacks in passing yards over the last four years. Still, his complete lack of rushing production has kept him outside the fantasy QB1 range in most of those seasons despite strong weapons and an excellent supporting cast.

Without rushing upside, even a big statistical season likely caps Goff in the same range as Tom Brady‘s heavy-volume 2021, which only produced a QB3 finish.

Goff is best treated as a streaming option rather than a draft-and-hold starter, valuable to pair with another quarterback and deploy on the best matchups each week.

Smith has been a dependable fantasy starter throughout his career, ranking among the top 30 wide receivers in fantasy points per game in each of the last four seasons despite playing as the second option behind A.J.

Brown. Smith has been at his best out wide, posting an 89.9 PFF receiving grade and 2.95 yards per route run there in 2025, tied for third-best in the league.

With Brown traded and Philadelphia's additions of Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown and Dontayvion Wicks profiling as slot options, Smith should play significantly more out wide while seeing a career-high target rate. His floor is safer than ever, and the Eagles rebounding as a team could push him into the top-five or top-10 conversation.

Collins owns a 92.7 PFF receiving grade over the last three seasons combined, tied for second-best among receivers. He scored 149.5 PPR points from Weeks 8 through 17 in 2025, seventh-best among wide receivers over that stretch.

The Texans' offensive overhaul, including a reworked offensive line and the addition of David Montgomery, gives reason for optimism that C.J. Stroud can bounce back from his 65.0 PFF grade in 2025. But Montgomery's presence could also mean significantly fewer pass attempts from a team that already plays with a top defense and little need to throw.

A season-ending ACL tear to Jayden Higgins will help Collins maintain a very high target rate this season, although the return of Tank Dell or Jaylin Noel stepping up could influence just how high his target rate can become. Collins has missed at least two games in each of his first five seasons. While his talent warrants early-round consideration, he carries more risk than most top-10 fantasy wide receiver options.

Mayfield has been a quality starter in Tampa Bay, peaking at fourth among fantasy quarterbacks in 2024 on the back of an unusually high touchdown rate and a jump in rushing. His 2025 slipped as the touchdown rate normalized and his accuracy fell, likely tied to oblique and shoulder injuries, though his rushing stayed strong.

A reasonable projection lands between those two seasons: Unlikely to repeat the 2024 touchdown spike, but with a higher rushing floor and a still-strong receiver group even without Mike Evans.

New coordinator Zac Robinson brings some uncertainty but has ties to the 2024 scheme, leaving Mayfield outside the top 12 but a strong later-round option who can start in the right matchups.

Hampton flashed his ceiling as a rookie with a 128-yard, one-touchdown outburst against the Giants. But an ankle fracture wiped out half his season, and his efficiency suffered behind a shaky offensive line. That line should be far better in 2026, with Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt back from injury and upgrades at center and right guard in Tyler Biadasz and Cole Strange.

The catch is a crowded backfield: Kimani Vidal impressed in Hampton's absence, and new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel pushed hard to sign Keaton Mitchell, the De'Von Achane-like back he just coached in Miami.

If McDaniel's offense takes off and Hampton secures the bulk of the touches, he has league-winning upside. But the touch distribution and a roster full of players returning from injury leave real risk.

Barkley was fantasy's top running back in 2024 at a historic, touchdown-heavy pace. He came back to earth last season, averaging 14.5 PPR points per game (15th among backs) as the entire Eagles offensive line took a step back.

With the line returning intact and Sean Mannion now calling plays, there's a path back toward his ceiling, but the real threat to his value is touch share.

Last year, Tank Bigsby out-graded and out-produced him on a per-touch basis last season, and at 29, Barkley is the one the Eagles might look to spell more often. Better per-touch efficiency wouldn't necessarily save Barkley’s fantasy value if it comes with fewer overall touches.

McBride had a historically great 2025, setting a new single-season record for receptions by a tight end and averaging 18.6 PPR points per game, sixth among all receivers.

Much of that was a product of circumstance: Arizona attempted a league-high 649 passes after losing its top two running backs in September and seeing five of its top eight wide receivers end the year on injured reserve. The good news is that Jacoby Brissett, who averaged a remarkable 21.

1 PPR points per game over his 12 starts, remains the expected starter, and a more balanced offense under new head coach Mike LaFleur should mean more red zone trips. The biggest worry is a mid-season quarterback change, since any replacement almost certainly won't feed McBride at the same rate.

Love has slipped from seventh to 21st among fantasy quarterbacks in points per game over three seasons, almost entirely because Green Bay's run-heavy approach has cut his passing volume. His grade remains elite, sitting fifth in the league over the past two years.

The ceiling is there if the Packers’ offense throws more, which is plausible given a strong young receiving group and a possibly weaker offensive line inviting more passing. That line is the real wild card, with two of its best pass protectors gone and several unproven starters remaining.

Love is a safe QB2 with top-10 upside, startable weekly in superflex and matchup-dependent elsewhere. He’s a potential weekly single-quarterback starter if Green Bay’s young pieces develop.

Willis has barely played in his career, amounting to just 118 dropbacks over the last two years. Yet when on the field, he grades well and, more importantly for fantasy, scrambles more often than any quarterback in the league.

The former Packer is now set to start for Miami. While some passing and rushing regression is fair to expect without his Green Bay supporting cast and against better-prepared defenses, his rushing floor alone gives him real fantasy upside.

Extrapolated over a full season, his Green Bay rushing rate would have led all quarterbacks. Willis is a strong target for anyone willing to wait on a second quarterback in redraft leagues.

Shough flashed as a rookie, averaging 17.6 PPR points per game as a starter with a strong blend of passing and rushing volume, but the production came against a soft schedule and with the Saints leaning heavily on him amid injuries and a thin supporting cast.

New Orleans added Travis Etienne and currently injured rookie Jordyn Tyson, which should help his efficiency but may also tilt the offense toward more rushing.

The likeliest outcome is mild regression even with better weapons, though there's real upside if the new pieces click. He's a strong late-round option and a good example of why waiting at quarterback makes sense in single-quarterback leagues.

Olave finished as the overall WR6 last season — driven by a career-high nine touchdowns — with his grades, catches and yardage otherwise in line with the two 1,000-yard seasons that opened his career.

Some regression is reasonable to expect, since he was the focal point of the offense late in the year while injuries and midseason departures thinned the group around him. Plus, New Orleans has since added first-round rookie Jordyn Tyson, even though he is currently injured, and signed Travis Etienne.

Olave has graded consistently across all four seasons, which makes him a steady mid-range WR1 and a weekly must-start when healthy. The catch is his concussion history: Five documented concussions make Olave more likely both to suffer another and to miss extended time if he does, so anyone drafting him needs a backup plan.

Pickens broke out in his first season with the Cowboys, finishing fifth in fantasy points and sixth in fantasy points per game after a career-high 2.

35 yards per route run, aided by a lower average depth of target that made more of his targets catchable and fueled 21 avoided tackles after the catch, fourth among wide receivers.

Some regression is likely, as his five touchdowns of over 25 yards were tied for the league lead; that kind of production is notoriously inconsistent from year to year. Despite the touchdown regression, he is still expected to be a consistent fantasy starter at worst, and a top-10 option at best.

Darnold grades among the league's best passers but finished just 27th in fantasy points per game last season, entirely because Seattle threw so little.

There's a real case for more volume this year: The backfield is thinner with Kenneth Walker III gone and Zach Charbonnet on the PUP, Rashid Shaheed has a full offseason with him and the league-best defense is likely to regress, all of which point to more passing.

The cap on Darnold’s upside is his rushing, with just 95 yards last season. He's a fine late-round option with genuine improvement potential, best deployed in weeks that project as competitive games.

Williams is one of four running backs to finish top 12 in fantasy points per game in each of the last three seasons.

He benefits from one of the league's best offenses in Los Angeles, where the Rams retained nearly their entire offensive unit and upgraded significantly on defense.

The only real ceiling concern is a drive-by-drive rotation with Blake Corum, who posted an identical 87.0 PFF rushing grade last season. Williams' edge as the better receiving back should keep him as the primary fantasy asset even if the split continues.

Stroud's grade and fantasy production have both slipped each year since a strong rookie season, but the biggest culprit has been Houston's offensive line: He's excellent when kept clean and merely average under pressure, which he's faced as often as almost any quarterback.

The line was reworked but still carries real questions, with a rookie draftee and two aging free agents. Stroud’s redraft outlook is poor, hurt further by a strong defense and added rushing that point to a conservative, low-volume offense.

The dynasty case is much better, since the young receiver group, an improving line, likely defensive regression and room for Stroud to grow as a passer could combine into a real leap in the next few years.

Wilson is a talented receiver coming off three straight 1,000-yard seasons and a strong start to 2025 that a knee injury cut short. His fantasy value has been capped mostly by poor Jets quarterback play, which new addition Geno Smith should help.

At the same time, Wilsonhe will face more target competition than he is used to after the team added Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper Jr. and Kenyon Sadiq.

His production is largely tied to overall offensive production: If New York clicks, he has clear top-10 upside, but if the unit is among the league's worst, he could fall outside the top 20.

Henry remains a high-end fantasy back when healthy, finishing eighth among running backs in points per game last season while scoring 16 rushing touchdowns for the second year in a row.

His minimal receiving role — tallying just 15 catches — caps his ceiling, and there is real regression risk. He turned 32 with a massive career workload, and the Ravens lost three of their best run-blockers in Tyler Linderbaum, Patrick Ricard and Charlie Kolar.

The offset is volume. No one on the depth chart is positioned to take carries from Henry, which keeps him a weekly must-start with low-end RB1 upside if everything goes well.

Jacobs has been a model of fantasy consistency, one of just eight backs to finish top-12 in points per game in both 2024 and 2025, and he carries the third-ranked PFF offensive grade over that span.

He has almost no competition for touches in Green Bay after Emanuel Wilson‘s departure, and an improving offensive line could finally lift the efficiency that a weak front had capped. The major caveats are durability and availability: Jacobs played through injury late in 2025 and was arrested on domestic violence allegations in May.

While he was released without charges, a suspension remains a real possibility. If the Green Bay offensive line takes a step forward and he stays available, Jacobs has league-winning upside, but the legal and disciplinary uncertainty makes him a genuine risk until there's more clarity.

Hall has been the Jets' lead back for three seasons but has slid from the overall RB2 in 2023 to outside the top 15, largely because his receiving role has shrunk.

That trend is unlikely to reverse under new playcaller Frank Reich, who has rarely featured his lead back in the passing game. Additionally, Braelon Allen‘s return could siphon goal-line work, capping the touchdown upside that is Hall's clearest path to a top-10 finish.

He remains the unquestioned starter on a team that will feed him volume, which keeps him a safe top-20 back, but his limited offensive ceiling holds back anything more. Hall has a groin strain, which shouldn't stop him from playing in Week 1, but will be an injury worth monitoring.

Flowers has been the focal point of Baltimore's passing game and a two-time Pro Bowler, standing out as the smaller, quicker yards-after-catch option in a receiving corps full of tall targets.

That size profile has limited his red-zone role and touchdown production, so he consistently ranks better in yardage than in fantasy points. There is added uncertainty this season under first-time offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, whose previous stops leaned on taller receivers, the same type Baltimore added in the draft.

He is still well worth a top-20 pick and should beat his ADP, though it is reasonable that Flowers has slipped behind receivers with more upside and better touchdown odds.

Love was selected third overall in April, the highest draft position for a running back since Saquon Barkley. Every running back taken within the first 20 picks over the past five seasons finished as a top-12 rookie. Love’s 79.2 PFF receiving grade ranks second among the top 20 running backs in the 2025 draft class, adding another dimension to an already high-upside profile.

The landing spot in Arizona is a mild concern given the existing backfield competition and a PFF run-blocking grade that ranked fourth-lowest in the NFL last season, but the draft capital alone should secure him enough volume to be a borderline RB1 in redrafts and the top option in dynasty rookie drafts.

Love is currently dealing with a high ankle sprain, which will likely impact his fantasy production the first month of the season, but ideally won't become a long term concern.

McMillan delivered a 1,000-yard rookie season as Carolina's clear top receiver and returns to rare continuity, keeping the same head coach, offensive coordinator and quarterback with little modification to his target competition.

His path to a top-10 ceiling runs through touchdowns: McMillan scored seven on a heavy share of the team's end-zone targets. Head coach Dave Canales has a history of funneling those looks to his top X receiver, the way Mike Evans and D.K.

Metcalf saw them at much higher rates under him. Still only 23 and drafted to take a modest step forward, the reigning Offensive Rookie of the Year profiles as a relatively safe WR2 with real upside if the scoring climbs.

Williams was excellent as a rookie backing up Melvin Gordon, but he tore his ACL and LCL early in 2022 after earning the starting job and hasn't looked the same since, including as Denver's primary back in 2024.

Dallas signed him in 2025, where he beat out Miles Sanders and rookie Jaydon Blue to be the feature back, played at least 70% of snaps in 11 of 16 games and averaged 15.2 fantasy points per game through Week 14. That placed 12th among running backs on a mix of efficiency and volume before a shoulder injury slowed his finish.

With the offense maintaining personnel and no new backfield additions, Williams projects for a similar role in 2026, leaning on Blue or Phil Mafah to spell him. His ceiling is capped, since it's unlikely he becomes a top-five back or that Dallas starts throwing to its backs more often, but he is a very safe RB2.

Bowers averaged at least 14.5 receiving PPR points per game in each of the last two seasons despite the Raiders posting the third-worst team PFF passing grade in the league over that span, a feat none of the other nine players to hit that threshold accomplished with a team passing grade in the bottom 12.

The top tight ends warrant high rankings in both redraft and dynasty because there is a higher correlation between fantasy points and PFF grades at tight end than at other positions. Bowers, Trey McBride and George Kittle all sit above 90.0 in PFF receiving grade over the last two years, with no one else clearing 85.0 on over 50 targets.

Kittle is working back from a torn Achilles, making McBride and Bowers the clear top two for now. The Raiders overhauled their roster around Bowers this offseason, adding head coach Klint Kubiak, quarterback Kirk Cousins and receiver Jalen Nailor. While the changes introduce some uncertainty, most of them point in a positive direction.

Nabers is one of the most talented wide receivers in the NFL, posting the best PFF receiving grade among wide receivers in the past two draft classes at 86.4. Further, his 29.

7% target rate led all wide receivers last season despite missing most of 2025 with a torn ACL. The unknown around his health heading into 2026 is the central issue, as most wide receivers see a significant production drop returning from a torn ACL.

The Giants signing Odell Beckham Jr., JuJu Smith-Schuster and Braxton Berrios in a single day signals the organization has real concerns about Nabers’ availability, making him a difficult top-10 pick despite the upside.

Rice was one of the most productive wide receivers per game last season at 18.8 PPR points, but he played just eight contests.

Further, his short-area role may be due for a change under Eric Bieniemy, whose offenses have historically featured receivers with much deeper target profiles. The off-field situation compounds the uncertainty, as Rice is rehabbing a knee surgery while serving a jail sentence.

He’s ended each of the last two seasons on injured reserve and carries additional off-field troubles that make him difficult to trust even at an ADP that already accounts for some of the risk.

McConkey impressed as a rookie before his production dipped in his second season, as a shift toward deep targets (where only four of his 17 were charted as catchable) increased competition from Keenan Allen, and a string of injuries cut into his efficiency and volume.

McConkey’s strength remains the intermediate game, where he earned a 90.0-plus PFF receiving grade on 10-to-19-yard-targets in both seasons.

New offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel should restore that usage, as his Miami offenses gave their top receiver at least 42 intermediate-range targets every season, with Jaylen Waddle and Tyreek Hill each topping 55 in a year. Improved health, reduced target competition and a scheme built for his strengths position McConkey for a career-best season.

Jones has been wildly inconsistent for fantasy across his career, and last season's strong 12th-place finish in Indianapolis leaned on five rushing touchdowns and an aggressive, high-aDOT passing profile rather than a real leap in passing quality.

His rushing volume has steadily declined, and a ruptured Achilles, even with a Week 1 return expected, makes another five-rushing-touchdown season unlikely.

The Colts also lost Michael Pittman Jr. and right tackle Braden Smith without meaningful additions, so the offense could slip. He's a fine second option in superflex but only a deep-bench consideration in single-quarterback redraft leagues.

Rodgers is well past his MVP peak, averaging fewer than 16 fantasy points per game in each of his past two seasons while posting the lowest full-season passing grade of his career in 2025.

A reunion with longtime head coach Mike McCarthy, along with the additions of Michael Pittman Jr. and Germie Bernard, should keep him from the bottom tier of fantasy quarterbacks, but at 42 years old, a meaningful rebound is unlikely.

Rodgers is strictly a superflex option, with the potential to provide steady QB2 production. The concern is that his continued decline could leave him unstartable even in that format.

Brissett is a career-long, borderline starter who posted a surprising ninth-place fantasy finish last season after taking over in Arizona, almost entirely on the back of massive passing volume in negative game scripts.

That volume is the worry: A healthier, upgraded backfield with Jeremiyah Love, Tyler Allgeier and James Conner should push Arizona toward the run, though a weak defense could still force plenty of late passing.

He's a viable short-term superflex option, but rookie Carson Beck looms as a late-season threat to his job. Anyone drafting Brissett should plan for the possibility he isn't the starter by the fantasy playoffs.

Burden excelled as a rookie despite never earning a full-time role, leading all Bears wide receivers with a 77.7 PFF receiving grade while finishing third among NFL wideouts in yards per route run (2.69) behind only Puka Nacua and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. His snap share, below 30% in the first half of the season, regularly exceeded 50% by year's end.

Chicago cleared his path to a starting job by trading DJ Moore and letting Olamide Zaccheaus walk, replacing them with only Kalif Raymond and a third-round rookie. Burden was especially dangerous in 12 personnel, generating 6.51 yards per route run, the best mark by any wide receiver in any personnel grouping with at least 40 routes.

The addition of rookie tight end Sam Roush could push the Bears further in that direction. The expanded role makes Burden a prime breakout candidate, particularly as a value in casual leagues. A groin injury shouldn't hurt Burden's ceiling, but if the injury lingers, it would impact his floor.

Egbuka had a turbulent, inconsistent rookie season, but much of the struggle traced to poor target quality on intermediate routes and a brutal late-season schedule rather than his own play. Indeed, barely a third of his deep intermediate targets even charted as catchable.

Both factors should ease in 2026 behind a healthier Baker Mayfield and a more balanced slate. New offensive coordinator Zac Robinson has slotted Egbuka as the offense's primary Z receiver, the same role that produced top-five fantasy seasons for Drake London, Puka Nacua and Cooper Kupp over the past five years.

Egbuka still has to win targets in a crowded room, but if he emerges as the clear No. 1, his role and environment give him one of the higher ceilings among receivers outside the elite tier.

Higgins is a talented, consistent piece of a Bengals passing game that returns almost entirely the same, catching passes from Joe Burrow in an offense that throws often.

The catch is his touchdown production: Higgins’ strong totals have come from sources that tend to regress, a cluster of long scores last season and a flood of short-yardage scores the year before.

Expecting double-digit touchdowns again is unrealistic, and with his injury history factored in, he shouldn't be drafted at his current ADP of WR15, which is exactly where he finished last season.

Young remains a work in progress, but improved weapons in 2025, highlighted by rookie Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker‘s breakout season, boosted his fantasy production even as his passing grade dipped slightly.

He still finished just 28th among quarterbacks in fantasy points per game, ahead of mostly displaced veterans and rookie starters, and Carolina made few meaningful additions to the offense this offseason.

At just 25 years old, Young still has time to develop, and this is a pivotal season for his future in Carolina, but several quarterbacks in his tier have improved their situations more significantly. He is a superflex-only option with little appeal in single-quarterback redraft leagues outside of very deep benches.

Waddle has been a top-15 fantasy wide receiver in his best seasons, and his PFF receiving grade bounced back to 85.2 in 2025. However, the move to Denver raises legitimate concerns about his ceiling. Sean Payton's offenses have historically underutilized smaller receivers, with most who started in his system failing to develop into reliable fantasy starters.

The Broncos also figure to be more run-heavy than the Saints teams Payton coached, with a top-six defense that will frequently keep them in winning positions without needing to throw the ball at a high rate.

The most likely outcome is that Waddle leads the team in targets while Courtland Sutton leads in touchdowns. That makes the former a high-floor WR3 with limited upside unless Denver is forced to throw more than expected.

McLaurin broke out to a WR7 finish in 2024 alongside Jayden Daniels, but 2025 was a letdown as injuries to both players and added competition from Deebo Samuel dropped him to 37th among receivers in points per game.

He remains Washington's clear top option entering 2026, and the late addition of Stefon Diggs should be workable given that McLaurin plays X while Diggs has recently worked from the slot and Z. He projects as a WR2 if the offense returns to 2024 form and a WR3 if it struggles.

New coordinator David Blough could move him around the formation more, though Diggs' arrival tempers that, leaving McLaurin more high-risk, high-reward than the safe weekly starter he's been in past years.

Judkins was Cleveland's lead back as a rookie but ran behind one of the league's worst offensive lines, dragging his efficiency to 3.6 yards per carry. The Browns overhauled that line this offseason, and while it may still grade below average, it should be far better than last year's unit.

Judkins is also coming off a season-ending ankle and fibula injury but has been a full participant this offseason and looks on track for Week 1, though there is some question about whether he will be at his usual standard right away.

If he returns to form behind the improved blocking and a larger workload, he profiles as a top-20 back. As long as the second-year rusher stays healthy, his volume alone should make him a trustworthy weekly fantasy starter.

Williams has been a true boom-or-bust receiver in Detroit, capable of huge yardage and touchdown games but prone to disappearing for stretches. That volatility persisted even as his overall production climbed in 2025 thanks to a higher snap rate and a more pass-heavy offense.

Williams has evolved from a pure deep threat into an elite after-the-catch weapon, ranking fourth among high-target receivers in yards after the catch over the last two seasons while doing so from a deeper target depth than the three players ahead of him.

His biggest limitation remains target competition, with Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta and Jahmyr Gibbs all soaking up touches, which keeps Williams right on the WR2/WR3 border. He should be a safe bet for another 1,000-yard season with a handful of touchdowns.

Tate was a surprise fourth overall pick in April, but the draft capital alone makes him the top dynasty rookie wide receiver and the first rookie wideout off the board in redrafts.

Recent top-10 selections like Ja'Marr Chase, Malik Nabers, Jaylen Waddle and Garrett Wilson all became immediate fantasy contributors. Tate's target share could mirror the 29.

8% Nabers generated in New York given Tennessee's similar receiver setup with Wan'Dale Robinson in the slot under Brian Daboll. The main variable is Cam Ward‘s development as a passer, but Tate has the role and the situation to be a fantasy starter from Day 1.

Irving has quietly become one of the league's most productive running backs over the past two seasons, grading near the top of the position while carrying one of its heaviest workloads.

His ADP took a hit from last season's injuries and an OTA setback, and it hasn't recovered even though he has been fully healthy since.

New offensive coordinator Zac Robinson should help, both by keeping the backs active in the passing game and by spreading goal-line work more evenly than Tampa Bay did last season. As long as he stays healthy, Irving projects as the clear lead back and a reliable fantasy starter even with Gainwell mixing in.

Moore is a remarkably consistent fantasy receiver, having finished top-36 in all eight of his seasons despite subpar quarterback play. A trade to Buffalo now pairs him with Josh Allen, the best quarterback of his career, plus reunites him with Joe Brady, under whom he had some of his best years.

The catch is that Brady spreads the ball around, which has suppressed even his top options. For example, Stefon Diggs‘ yards per game nearly halved after Brady took over, and Moore is coming off across-the-board career lows.

That lands him in the WR3 tier — generally high upside with real risk — though near the top of it given his long history of ending as a WR3 at worst.

Adams has been a fantasy starter for a decade, but at 34 with a steadily declining grade, his top-10 days are likely behind him.

He still finished top 10 in points per game last season, though almost entirely on the back of a league-high 14 touchdowns and a historic 57.4% share of the Rams' end-zone targets, production that rarely repeats year to year.

With touchdown regression likely, a possible smaller role as Terrance Ferguson emerges and modest receptions and yardage underneath, he profiles as a boom-or-bust WR3 whose weekly value hinges on finding the end zone.

Watson broke out late last season as clearly the best receiver in a crowded Green Bay room, pairing an elite grade with a WR12 finish over the closing weeks despite missing half the year with a torn ACL.

The Packers have since thinned that room and signed him to a large extension, making him their unquestioned top target with far less competition.

Watson’s ceiling is legitimate WR1 production if he stays healthy, but a long history of knee, hamstring and now ACL injuries keeps the risk high.

Washington broke out late last season, taking over the slot in Liam Coen's offense and posting a strong finish through the playoffs while also displaying the ability to produce on the outside.

He returns to a crowded Jacksonville receiver room but projects as one of the team's top two targets alongside Brian Thomas Jr. Coen's track record with elite fantasy receivers gives him real appeal, but a balanced, run-leaning offense makes Washington more of a boom-or-bust play than a steady weekly producer.

Loveland was a rare top-10 pick at tight end. After a slow start, he caught fire late, posting four 90-yard games (including the playoffs) — no other tight end tallied more than three. That surge fueled an 86.

2 PFF receiving grade, among the best at the position. With Chicago thinning its receiver room by moving on from DJ Moore and Olamide Zaccheaus, Loveland should see steadier target volume in a Ben Johnson offense.

He has the talent and upside to finish as the No. 1 tight end, though his production was concentrated over a short window, which makes him more regression-prone than steadier options like Brock Bowers and Trey McBride and keeps him just outside the top tier.

Kraft was the NFL's most efficient tight end in 2024, leading the position at 9.3 yards per target, but volume held him back. Green Bay leaned on him more in 2025, and his target rate jumped to 19.1% while his 10.

8 yards after the catch per reception set a record for tight ends in PFF's 20 years of charting. He was averaging 14.7 PPR points per game, tied for second among tight ends, before a season-ending ACL injury cut things short.

With Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks gone and no meaningful additions at receiver, the targets are there for the taking. If Kraft returns to full health, he has a realistic path to a top-three finish in 2026.

Odunze looked like a budding star through four weeks last season, accumulating five touchdowns and a WR3 pace before a foot injury that first showed up around Week 9 sapped his production (two or fewer catches in five of his next seven games) and eventually cost him the final five games of the regular season.

He returned for the playoffs at limited capacity, and while DJ Moore is now gone, Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland both closed the season as legitimate weapons, obscuring the target hierarchy in 2026. Odunze says his foot feels different but no longer limits him.

He should be part of a clear top three in targets with Burden and Loveland, though the order among them is genuinely uncertain. He carries top-10 upside but real risk of inconsistency, which is the normal range for a player drafted as a WR3.

Evans arrives in San Francisco at 33, coming off an injury-marred final season in Tampa Bay but bringing a decade of elite, touchdown-heavy production.

He owns the only secure role in a rebuilt 49ers receiver room, though his snaps could slip in run-first situations as his blocking fades with age.

Evans’ appeal is touchdown volume in a Kyle Shanahan offense that consistently ranks among the best, but his value is contingent on how much playing time he keeps and whether he still dominates red-zone targets.

Ward's rookie year was undercut by injuries and turnover around him, with Calvin Ridley missing most of the season, Tyler Lockett requesting his release and his head coach fired six games in.

He finished strong, though, producing multiple touchdowns in each of his final four full games and his best grades late. A rebuilt supporting cast in Carnell Tate, Wan'Dale Robinson and a healthy Ridley, plus new coordinator Brian Daboll, sets up a cleaner Year 2.

He isn't worth drafting in most single-quarterback redraft leagues but is a strong waiver target with a good start and a worthwhile upside pick in superflex.

Fannin was excellent as a rookie, finishing the year as Cleveland's focal point with a top-five PFF receiving grade among high-volume tight ends.

His outlook improves under new head coach Todd Monken, whose offenses have consistently ranked near the top in tight end touchdowns, and his role is now locked in with David Njoku gone.

The main caution is the Browns' investment in receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston, which could pull some targets away. Fannin’s talent and heavy volume give him real upside into the elite tier, but for now, enough tight ends in better offenses with superior quarterbacks rank slightly ahead of him.

Smith returns to where his career began, taking over as the Jets‘ starting quarterback after three productive seasons in Seattle and a disappointing year in Las Vegas. His peak came in 2022, when he finished fifth among fantasy quarterbacks, though his fantasy points per game declined in each of the following seasons.

Last year was another step back, as his passing yards per game dropped by 40 from his 2023 mark following the midseason trade of Jakobi Meyers, a knee injury to Brock Bowers and the firing of offensive coordinator Chip Kelly.

New York's supporting cast, led by Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell and rookies Omar Cooper Jr. and Kenyon Sadiq, is stronger than what he had in Las Vegas but falls short of the prime D.K. Metcalf-Tyler Lockett pairing, and at 36 years old, Smith no longer offers much rushing upside. He is best avoided in single-quarterback redraft leagues and profiles as a safe, low-end QB2 in superflex formats.

LaPorta has quietly been one of the best non-elite tight ends in football, ranking top 10 in fantasy points per game each of the last two years and top five in touchdowns over three seasons despite a target rate held down by heavy competition from Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams and Jahmyr Gibbs.

New coordinator Drew Petzing's track record of funneling targets to tight ends in both Cleveland and Arizona is a real reason to expect LaPorta’s usage to improve.

The swing factor is health, since a string of injuries culminated in offseason back surgery, but he looks on track for Week 1. If he stays healthy, LaPorta has a real shot at climbing into the tight end position's top tier.

Swift posted modest RB2 production each of the last two seasons in Chicago. Although better offensive line play helped his per-touch efficiency improve significantly last season, rookie Kyle Monangai cut into his snap share enough that his fantasy points per game barely moved.

Some of that good line play could regress in the short term with starting center Drew Dalman‘s retirement, and added receiver competition for carries is another mild headwind. But Swift still graded clearly better than Monangai as a runner, receiver and pass-blocker, making a real role change unlikely.

If anything, he might see more touches early in the season as Monangai deals with a hyperextended knee. Between his age, workload history and clear edge in skill over his main competition, Swift projects as a low-end RB2 again, about as safe a bet at the position as you'll find beyond the first few rounds.

Montgomery has quietly been one of the league's most productive backs over the past two seasons, held back in Detroit only by the presence of Jahmyr Gibbs.

Houston traded for him and revised his contract this offseason, and with minimal backfield competition, he should command a significant workload behind a defense strong enough to keep him in favorable game scripts. The main worry is Houston's run-blocking, which ranked 21st last season, though the Texans made offseason upgrades.

Plus, Montgomery is among the best in the league at creating yards through contact. If he locks in a true lead-back role, he profiles as one of the biggest values relative to his ADP. Even in a committee, he remains a viable starter in most formats.

Many fantasy managers wrote Stevenson off after New England drafted TreVeyon Henderson in the second round, but offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels has always run committee backfields, and Stevenson held the clear lead in touches down the stretch last season.

He remains the more physical runner and grades better in short-yardage, goal-line, receiving and pass protection, and the Patriots did nothing this offseason to add real competition.

With his ADP outside the top 30, Stevenson profiles as a robust value, especially if Henderson doesn't take a major leap and the backfield stays split the way it finished last year.

Etienne lands in New Orleans on a top-of-market contract that locks him in as the starter and should guarantee top-20 volume.

The concern is efficiency: He leaves a mediocre Jacksonville run-blocking unit for a Saints line that ranked 31st, which could push his yards per carry below 4.0.

Plus, Kellen Moore‘s offenses have a consistent track record of suppressing their lead back's receiving numbers. That combination gives him a fairly safe floor as a top-20 back but a capped limit unless the Saints' line and offense take a real step forward.

Warren, the 14th overall pick in 2025, looked like a league winner early, ranking third among tight ends in fantasy points and leading the position in receiving yards through seven weeks.

However, his production cratered over the final 10 weeks as the Colts‘ offense declined, with Daniel Jones‘ passing grade sliding and a midseason quarterback carousel that even included a brief Philip Rivers cameo.

IIf Jones bounces back from his torn Achilles, Warren has elite upside. However, he has significant competition for underneath targets from Josh Downs and Keenan Allen. Even if Jones disappoints, the added targets should lift Warren from 13th over the back half of 2025 into the top 12.

Pitts broke out in 2025 with a much larger role, finishing fifth among tight ends in fantasy points per game.

However, a new coaching staff, added competition and quarterback uncertainty cloud his 2026 outlook.

He is worth a top-10 tight end pick with top-five upside, though he could fall outside the top 12 if the new regime doesn't feature him.

Kittle is one of fantasy's elite tight ends when healthy, with a top-six finish in points per game in each of the past eight seasons. The problem is the Achilles tear he suffered in the wild-card game, on top of a career-long injury history and an age-33 season ahead.

He's pushing to play Week 1, but returning is not the same as producing, and his slow start after last year's hamstring absence is a useful warning.

Kittle carries the last real overall TE1 potential on the board, but anyone drafting him needs a more stable second option to cover the early weeks.

Metcalf has been a productive receiver his whole career but has slipped from his 2020 peak. His first year in Pittsburgh brought his lowest yardage and receptions since his rookie season, largely because of the offense's low passing volume.

The upside is a scheme change: Arthur Smith is out, and new coach Mike McCarthy has run far more pass-heavy offenses.

The offsets are more target competition after Pittsburgh added Michael Pittman Jr. and two drafted receivers, and an aging Aaron Rodgers could decline further and prompt a more conservative approach. Metcalf is a fine flex option as his offense's top target, but a big production jump from last season is unlikely.

Kelce's production has slid from perennial TE1 to the back half of the top 10, but even in a down 2025, he finished ninth among tight ends in points per game and stayed a central part of the offense.

At 37 and unlikely to rebound in efficiency, he still profiles for significant volume given that Kansas City did little to replace its departed pass-catchers, and the return of former coordinator Eric Bieniemy could nudge his target rate up.

Kelce is worth drafting as a starter but as a set-and-forget streamer-plus rather than a top-five option, owning some risk of falling outside the top 12 if age catches up and other borderline options hit.

Skattebo flashed lead-back ability as a rookie, averaging 19.2 fantasy points per game across a four-start stretch before suffering a season-ending injury in Week 8 that included a dislocated ankle, fractured fibula and ruptured deltoid ligament. New York initially added little competition to the backfield, but the free-agent signing of Najee Harris complicates the outlook.

Harbaugh and Matt Nagy have both leaned on committee backfields, and Harbaugh has a long history of utilizing bigger backs in Baltimore. Skattebo should still lead the Giants in carries and remains the better fantasy option of the two, but Harris adds another obstacle to a true workhorse role.

The bigger issue is Skattebo’s price. He is being drafted ahead of backs such as Bucky Irving, Quinshon Judkins and D'Andre Swift, who either play in better offenses with more secure volume or have clearer paths to workhorse roles.

Wilson looked squeezed out of Arizona's lineup early last season, but a wave of injuries thrust him into a full-time X role, where he exploded for the second-most PPR points among receivers over the final eight weeks.

New head coach Mike LaFleur has said Wilson will play the Puka Nacua role, and his late-season route profile already began to mirror Nacua's.

He isn't the talent Nacua is, has a lesser quarterback and will cede targets to Trey McBride, so a repeat of that top-five stretch is unlikely. Still, that responsibility should support solid production, making him a weekly flex with WR2 upside if he plays well.

Henderson flashed real upside as a rookie, including a dominant two-week stretch. But Josh McDaniels has a long history of splitting his backfield, and Rhamondre Stevenson graded better as a runner, receiver and pass-blocker.

With no meaningful offseason additions to the backfield, the likeliest outcome is another committee in which Stevenson leads and Henderson's value spikes mainly in blowouts.

The upside case is that Henderson improves as a pass protector and takes over the passing-down work, which could make both backs startable or even push Henderson into weekly must-start territory.

Tuten showcased efficiency as a rookie with strong yards-after-contact, first-down and avoided-tackle rates, and his poor yards-before-contact mark points to bad run-blocking rather than his own play.

The concern is volume: Jacksonville replaced Travis Etienne with the statistically similar Chris Rodriguez, and all signs point to a three-man rotation with LeQuint Allen.

Tuten is the likeliest fantasy option of the group, but the range of outcomes is wide, and this could be a pass-first offense that splits carries evenly enough that no back is weekly-reliable. He is going as a low-end RB2, a price that carries real risk.

Harrison entered the league as a heralded prospect but has been an inconsistent, touchdown-dependent producer across two seasons, finishing as WR30 and 27th in PPR points while never breaking out the way his draft billing suggested.

His quarterback situation doesn't fully explain it, since his per-game production was identical with Kyler Murray and Jacoby Brissett, and an injury-marred stretch last season saw Michael Wilson outproduce anything Harrison has managed.

New coach Mike LaFleur plans to use Harrison in the Davante Adams role, a stylistic change from his current route profile that could either unlock him or leave him with Adams' modest volume and fewer touchdowns. He is best viewed as a high-risk, high-reward flex option.

Pollard is one of two running backs with four straight 1,000-yard rushing seasons. Despite average rate stats on the surface, his 3.3 yards after contact per carry over the last four years ties for fourth among backs with at least 500 carries, suggesting a talented runner held back by his situation rather than a mediocre one.

The good news for 2026 is the Titans passed on Jeremiyah Love at fourth overall to take wide receiver Carnell Tate, and their only backfield additions being Michael Carter and fifth-round rookie Nicholas Singleton. If everything stays the same, Pollard profiles as a low-end RB2, but there is real upside if the offense improves, with Peter Skoronski and JC Latham still developing up front and Cam Ward showing meaningful late-season growth in his rookie year.

A few more touchdowns alone would push Pollard into mid-range RB2 territory, and a better offensive line on top of that would bring him closer to a top-10 fantasy back. However, the first two preseason games made the backfield look more split than it had been in the past two seasons, with Tyjae Spears playing more snaps with the starters than Pollard.

Dowdle parlayed a breakout stretch as Carolina's starter into a Pittsburgh contract, reconnecting with Mike McCarthy, his head coach for five seasons in Dallas.

He steps into a genuine timeshare with Jaylen Warren, who grades out as the better back, especially as a receiver, though the rushing gap is narrow.

The likeliest outcome is a committee, possibly with Dowdle leaning early-down and Warren on passing downs, and the familiarity with McCarthy could tilt usage Dowdle’s way. He is worth a selection among the top 30 running backs, since most scenarios leave him a flex option at worst and a weekly RB2 at best.

Thomas exploded as a rookie, finishing fourth among receivers in total PPR points, but his production dipped in year two as Travis Hunter pushed him out of the slot, his average depth of target climbed and his target rate fell.

Thomas enters this season with the same coach and quarterback, a role that is not expected to change and clear signs of improved chemistry with Lawrence from OTAs and training camp.

He is a strong bounce-back candidate, aided by likely positive touchdown regression, though a deep Jacksonville receiving group makes him a boom-or-bust play week to week. The likeliest outcome is a much stronger third season, even if the raw numbers fall short of his rookie totals.

Kincaid ranks sixth in PFF receiving grade, first in target rate and second in yards after the catch per reception among tight ends with at least 400 routes over the past two seasons. Only George Kittle slots ahead of him in yards per route run, making him one of the most talented receiving tight ends in the league when healthy.

The problem is that Kincaid has played just 12 games at 37.6% of offensive snaps on average over the past two seasons due to a torn PCL. While he has opted against surgery on doctors' advice and says he feels significantly better, the Bills' coaching staff has publicly acknowledged ongoing uncertainty about his week-to-week availability.

In his favor, Kincaid owns one of the strongest quarterback situations among fantasy tight ends outside the elite tier, paired with Josh Allen in an offense that added DJ Moore but should otherwise remain intact. If healthy, his ceiling is among the top fantasy tight ends, but pairing him with a safer secondary option is essentially required given the durability concerns.

Price was the second-best running back in the 2026 class despite limited collegiate experience as a backup.

Seattle's run-heavy offense with 439 carries last season gives him a clear path to immediate starter volume after the Seahawks lost Kenneth Walker III in free agency and Zach Charbonnet to an ACL injury in the playoffs.

The concern is that Seattle's backfield split last season made neither Walker nor Charbonnet fully trustworthy in fantasy, and Price's lack of receiving experience could keep him in a similar early-down role even if he leads the team in carries.

Andrews was a must-start tight end for six straight seasons but slipped to 24th in points per game last year, hurt by fewer receptions, only five touchdowns and a dip in efficiency that was partly tied to Lamar Jackson‘s injury.

His 2026 outlook is brighter: With Isaiah Likely and Charlie Kolar both gone, Andrews’ playing time should climb notably, and a new coaching staff has already labeled him a focal point of the offense.

He should be the clear second target-earner in one of the league's most promising offenses, with real bounce-back potential. Given Andrews’ heavily discounted ADP, he's a strong value with top-five upside if the decline doesn't continue.

Pittman is coming off a down year, hampered by a 2024 back injury and then squeezed in 2025 by Indianapolis' emerging pass-catchers. A trade to Pittsburgh gives him a fresh start.

The scheme change helps: New coach Mike McCarthy runs a pass-heavier offense than Arthur Smith did, and the underneath, possession profile McCarthy has historically fed profiles more like Pittman than D.K. Metcalf.

The risks are a 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers who could decline further and a possible push from rookie Germie Bernard for the second receiver job. Pittman is a flex option with upside as Pittsburgh's top target, but genuine downside if he slides to a rotational role.

Robinson broke out as a high-volume slot receiver in New York, setting a career high in yards per route run in 2025 after Malik Nabers‘ injury opened up a bigger role.

He followed play-caller Brian Daboll to Tennessee on a four-year deal, which is a plus for his usage, but he lands in a far more crowded receiver room than he had with the Giants.

With rookie Carnell Tate, Calvin Ridley and others ahead of or alongside him, Robinson’s role could shrink back to slot-only work, hindering both his routes and his target rate. Robinson should see enough volume to be a weekly flex, but his upside is constricted as long as the rest of the group stays healthy.

Godwin was on his way to a career year in 2024, ranking second among receivers in points per game in Liam Coen's offense before a dislocated ankle ended his season, and the injury lingered into a limited 2025.

He returns to a crowded Tampa Bay receiver room, but the offense should resemble the 2024 version that suited him, now run by Coen disciple Zac Robinson. The catch is target competition, especially from emerging second-year man Emeka Egbuka, which gives Godwin an unusually wide range of outcomes.

He could be the team's most talented and experienced receiver or slip to third or fourth in the pecking order, so his fantasy value hinges on how the rotation sorts out.

Likely has been an efficient but low-volume tight end, buried behind Mark Andrews in Baltimore yet posting elite per-target grades. He reunites with John Harbaugh in New York on a top-six tight end contract and walks into real opportunity.

Jaxson Dart targets tight ends far more than the Giants' other quarterbacks did, and Malik Nabers‘ uncertain ACL recovery could open a path for Likely to lead the team in targets.
