If Likely’s efficiency holds on a much larger workload, he has legitimate top-tier ability, making him a borderline starter and an ideal target for managers who wait at tight end. However, in the first preseason game, he was part of a rotation in 11 personnel. If that carries on into the regular season, that immediately puts a ceiling on his potential.

Ferguson has been Dallas' primary tight end for three seasons, making two Pro Bowls and finishing 10th, 24th and 10th in fantasy points per game. His value is tied to CeeDee Lamb‘s absence, as he was the top tight end in football from Weeks 3 to 8 last season at 16.

1 PPR points per game while Lamb was hurt, then fell to 8.3 once the offense was whole. Ferguson’s 60.0 PFF receiving grade ranked fourth-lowest among 29 tight ends with at least 300 routes run, which would normally put a job at risk.

However, Dallas added no tight end help beyond undrafted free agents and brings back the same coaches, quarterback and target competition, so his role is secure. Ferguson is a safe low-end starter or high-end backup whose floor beats most tight ends at a similar ADP, even if he risks finishing outside the top 12 without enough touchdowns.

Warren has steadily grown his role in Pittsburgh since going undrafted in 2022, grading out ahead of both Najee Harris and now Rico Dowdle.

His 2026 outlook is cloudier with Mike McCarthy taking over as head coach and bringing in Dowdle, setting up a committee in which the rushing bridge is narrow but Warren holds a clear edge as a receiver.

A split is the likeliest outcome, possibly orienting Warren toward passing downs, though the backfield could break either way. He is worth a selection among the top 30 running backs, since most scenarios leave him a flex option at worst and a weekly RB2 at best.

Downs has been quietly excellent across his first three seasons as the Colts' slot receiver, earning an 82.5 PFF grade and ranking among the top 30 in yards per route run. The catch for fantasy has been usage: Stuck in 11 personnel behind Alec Pierce and Michael Pittman Jr., he played just 58.

7% of snaps last season, well below the 80%-plus that most startable receivers see. After Indianapolis traded Pittman to Pittsburgh, Downs was bumped to second on the depth chart, and general manager Chris Ballard has publicly endorsed a bigger role.

His upside took a hit when the Colts signed Keenan Allen, but Allen is 34 and only played 55% of snaps last season. We could see Downs play outside in 12 personnel and in the slot in 11, with Allen joining for 11 personnel only. Downs will likely remain a value at his ADP given good quality of play in the past, and likely increase in playing time.

Sutton has been Denver's top receiver and a touchdown machine under Sean Payton, tallying the sixth-most receiving scores in the league over the past three seasons.

The question is a crowded room: The Broncos traded for Jaylen Waddle and still have three young receivers they've invested in, and Payton has a long history of rotating the position.

At 31 with a strong grade chasm behind Waddle and a rookie in Pat Bryant capable of pushing him at X, Sutton's volume could erode, and Denver may move on after the season. He remains a touchdown-dependent flex option, with his outlook tied largely to how the rotation shakes out.

Pierce broke out in 2025 with 1,003 yards and six touchdowns despite only 51 of his 83 targets being catchable. Those numbers were a product of his 20.1-yard average depth of target.

He finished as WR27 with seven top-24 weeks but also four outside the top 50, illustrating the boom-or-bust nature of a deep-target receiver with a modest target rate. Pierce’s four-year, $116 million contract extension signaled an increased role in the offense, but Pierce has spent training camp on the PUP.

The Colts signed Keenan Allen to replace Michael Pittman Jr., giving Indianapolis a third underneath target joining Josh Downs and Tyler Warren. It's unlikely Pierce will see a significantly increased role after the addition of Allen, leaving him as a high-risk, high-reward target once he is healthy.

Lemon is an undersized but heavily slot-tested rookie who should immediately become Philadelphia's primary slot receiver, working behind DeVonta Smith on the outside and likely seeing more targets than Dontayvion Wicks despite less raw playing time.

The fit isn't perfect, since the Eagles have historically been one of the league's lightest slot-target offenses and new coordinator Sean Mannion‘s history is only average to slightly below in that department, but some uptick from recent years is still expected.

As a run-heavy team's likely second receiving option as a rookie, Lemon's ceiling depends on quickly proving he belongs, though A.J. Brown and Smith's recent top-20 finishes show real upside exists in this passing game if he gets there. The first-round pick profiles as a high-risk, high-reward low-end WR3 or high-end WR4 for his rookie season.

Reed has been one of the most productive slot receivers in the league over the past three seasons, but his fantasy value has been capped by Green Bay's refusal to use him in two-receiver sets, a low 11-personnel rate and run-heavy game scripts in wins.

A collarbone and foot injury wiped out most of his 2025. The reason for optimism is that Green Bay thinned its outside depth by moving on from Dontayvion Wicks and Romeo Doubs without acquiring a notable replacement, which could earn Reed more two-receiver-set snaps.

That gives him a path to a more reliable flex role, with definite potential if Matthew Golden or Christian Watson falters.

Worthy flashed real promise as a rookie once the Chiefs moved him into the slot, closing the year strong through the playoffs. However, his 2025 was derailed by a Week 1 shoulder injury he played through all season and only had surgery on afterward.

That context reframes his down year, and the Chiefs signaled continued faith by moving on from Hollywood Brown and JuJu Smith-Schuster without adding meaningful competition. Still very young and now paired with new coordinator Eric Bieniemy, whose offense historically centers around a Tyreek Hill-type speedster, Worthy has a clear path to leading Kansas City in receiving.

He re-sprained his shoulder at the start of training camp, causing him to miss most of camp, and lowering Worthy's floor this season. He profiles as a flex option if healthy with top-10 upside if he becomes the Chiefs’ top weapon.

Brooks entered the league as the top running back of the 2024 class with no clear weaknesses in his profile, but two ACL tears in the same right knee wiped out most of two seasons.

Carolina shut him down for all of 2025 to protect him and didn't meaningfully replace Rico Dowdle, a sign the team is counting on him. The initial thought is Brooks could be eased in and then eventually earn the starting job.

Chuba Hubbard suffered a hamstring injury in the middle of training camp, which further opens the door for Brooks to take the starting job, leading to his ADP to quickly rise. He should remain a steal in home leagues as long as his ADP is slow to adjust, but it's hard to know how valuable he will be until his ADP stabilizes.

Johnston has been a boom-or-bust, touchdown-dependent receiver through two seasons, pairing occasional big games with long stretches of minimal production. He finished just 39th in points per game last year despite scoring eight touchdowns.

The optimism for 2026 comes from new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, whose speed-based scheme fits Johnston's play style well and could lower his average depth of target enough to lift his catch rate and efficiency.

The offset is target volume, with Los Angeles investing in the run game and tight ends as well as carrying other promising receivers in Ladd McConkey and Tre Harris. The likeliest outcome is another frustrating, touchdown-reliant flex, though a real leap into weekly-starter territory is on the table.

Diggs was elite in his prime and remains highly efficient, ranking fifth among receivers in yards per route run last season while playing barely half of New England's snaps. The Patriots moved on anyway, trading for A.J. Brown and signing Romeo Doubs, with offseason legal issues likely factoring in.

Diggs signed with the Washington Commanders during training camp, where he instantly became the second wide receiver option behind Terry McLaurin. It's unlikely his target rate will be as high with McLaurin on the roster, and less probable he will see as accurate of passes from Jayden Daniels as he saw from Drake Maye.

Diggs' age is also a risk, as he will be 33 before the season starts. The second preseason game suggested Diggs will only play in 11 personnel, so his snap rate will be similar to last season. Still, his talent mixed with a decent target rate can still make him a flex option, or potentially a weekly starter if all goes well.

Coker went from undrafted out of Holy Cross to a real role in Carolina, grading noticeably better than Xavier Legette in each of his two seasons and closing 2025 with two strong, high-snap games in the finale and wild-card round.

The Panthers gave him a three-year extension they didn't have to, all but locking in a full-time role.

He is worth a late-round flier in case Carolina's offense improves enough to support a second fantasy-relevant receiver alongside Tetairoa McMillan.

Concepcion enters the NFL as a quick, versatile receiver who lined up all over the formation at Texas A&M, drawing a player comparison to Luther Burden III.

He was placed in arguably the best possible spot for early volume: Cleveland had the league's biggest receiver need and returns essentially the same room that posted the lowest team PFF receiving grade in football, with Jerry Jeudy the only holdover who topped 25 catches last year.

New head coach Todd Monken arrives from Baltimore, where Zay Flowers anchored the passing game, and Concepcion is the closest thing the Browns have to that role. That gives the rookie a real path to leading the team in targets and strong near-term upside, though his long-term outlook is cloudier with more receiver investment likely coming.

Goedert has been a reliable fantasy tight end for years, finishing top 12 in points or points per game every season since his second, mostly on volume that gave him a high floor and low ceiling. His 2025 campaign was the worst of his career by most measures, with career lows in PFF receiving grade (69.7), yards per game (39.4), yards per reception, yards after catch and big-play rate.

Goedert stayed fantasy-relevant only because of a career-high 11 receiving touchdowns, but that total rests on extreme outliers: Eight came inside the 6-yard line (tied for the most by a tight end in 20 years) and five arrived via shovel passes and wide screens (more than double any tight end over that span), which makes heavy regression likely.

With the Eagles drafting Eli Stowers to cut into his snaps and Sean Mannion taking over as offensive coordinator, Goedert will need both a bounce-back in quality of play and continued scheme help to avoid sliding into bye-week fill-in territory.

Gainwell broke out as a receiving back in Pittsburgh last season, ranking fifth among running backs in receiving yards and fourth in receptions while flashing standalone value in two starts.

He moved to Tampa Bay this offseason, where his target rate should land between his Philadelphia and Pittsburgh levels. Gainwell’s fantasy value relies on more than the receiving role: The real potential is overtaking Bucky Irving, as Irving did not appear to be the same player last season after his injuries.

Gainwell is best viewed as one of the top handcuffs available, thanks to his quality play and elevated odds of seizing the starting job.

Shaheed has built a career as an explosive, boom-or-bust deep threat, with big plays and touchdowns offset by frequent quiet games, and a meniscus tear ended his 2024 early.

A 2025 trade sent him to Seattle to reunite with coordinator Klint Kubiak, though his role and average depth of target dipped there.

The Seahawks changed coordinators again but signed him long-term, and there is real buzz he could leap Cooper Kupp to become the clear second option behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba. He is a high-upside late-round pick, with the bonus that his fantasy outlook should clarify within the first month or two.

Dobbins has been highly effective everywhere he has played with a career 5.2 yards-per-carry mark, and he enters the season atop Denver's depth chart.

The catch is volume and health: The Broncos added Jonah Coleman and can lean more on R.J. Harvey. Dobbins’ carries should shrink, and a long injury history has cost him significant time in nearly every season.

His upside is capped because Denver has shown it will spread the backfield around rather than funnel work to one back. That leaves him a solid but low-ceiling flex option when healthy.

Boston improved each year at Washington and profiles as an X receiver who has also found success in limited snaps elsewhere, with his hands and competitive toughness rated as his best traits.

Cleveland took him 39th overall, not long after KC Concepcion, and the two fit together well since Concepcion projects more as a Z or slot option, with Jerry Jeudy also more experienced inside. The likeliest outcome is that those three lead the position in playing time, with Isaiah Bond the main threat to push Boston to fourth.

New head coach Todd Monken is a mixed signal, since X receivers didn't produce much for him in Baltimore, but he was the Tampa Bay coordinator during Mike Evans' only 1,300-yard seasons. Boston is a strong late-round option who probably shouldn't start early, though the upside is real on a team that may need to throw often.

Hubbard has outlasted a steady stream of backfield competition in Carolina, including D'Onta Foreman, Miles Sanders and Rico Dowdle, and his 2024 campaign brought career highs across the board. Last season was a step back, as a declining grade and strong stretches from Dowdle pushed him into a backup role for much of the second half.

Dowdle is gone, but Jonathon Brooks is back after two ACL tears cost him nearly all of his first two seasons, and a training camp hamstring injury for Hubbard gives Brooks extended time with the starters this preseason.

That makes him a calculated risk worth taking, especially for managers who need early-season running back help, and his slipping ADP could turn him into a late-round value.

A second-round pick in 2019, he authored one of the most unusual fantasy seasons in NFL history in 2021, finishing as a top-five wide receiver as a downfield weapon for half the year and as a part-time running back for the other half.

Every season since has been a strong start followed by injuries, including last year in Washington, where he was WR7 through five weeks before a heel problem and Jayden Daniels‘ absence dropped him to 33rd in points per game.

San Francisco brought him back this offseason, and Ricky Pearsall‘s surgery and move to injured reserve clears the way for him to reclaim the Z role. He is worth a mid-to-late-round pick and should start weekly when healthy, which has always been the question.

Golden was thrust into significant playing time as a rookie thanks to a steady stream of injuries around him, bouncing from Z to the slot to a late-season X rotation with Romeo Doubs as the receiving corps shuffled.

With Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks both gone and Green Bay notably skipping the position in the draft, Golden enters 2026 as the starting X receiver alongside Christian Watson and Jayden Reed.

He may open the season lower in the target pecking order, but durability concerns up and down Green Bay's skill positions, including Tucker Kraft, Josh Jacobs and the injury-prone Watson, give him a real path to a bigger role if the injuries continue.

Doubs has long been a borderline redraft receiver as a steady, touchdown-capable option who finished 45th in points per game last season, and a move to New England clouds his role.

He is likely to land in a Stefon Diggs-type job, some Z and some slot, behind an X group that now includes A.J. Brown and Kyle Williams.

However, Doubs’ sizable contract suggests the Patriots will give him a real shot. That makes him a fine late-round flex, particularly valuable as a safer complement for anyone who has taken several risks at receiver.

Meyers has been a quietly reliable receiver for years, climbing to a WR19 finish in 2024 before a midseason trade to Jacksonville and a dip to WR32 in 2025.

He took over as the Jaguars' Z receiver down the stretch and led their wideouts in routes and receptions, though Parker Washington outproduced him.

Meyers’ best case is a full offseason in the offense pushing him toward a top-20 finish, but the path is muddied: A returning Travis Hunter, a rising Washington, positive camp buzz around others and more two-tight-end sets all threaten his playing time. The likeliest outcome is a flex option rather than a weekly must-start.

Since 2022, Mason ranks third among running backs with at least 300 carries in yards per carry, yards after contact per carry and first down or touchdown rate. He is the only back in that group with a positive grade on over half of his runs, making him one of the most efficient runners in the league.

Mason averaged 14.5 PPR points per game in his four starts last season with Minnesota, and with Aaron Jones now 31 and having missed at least five contests in two of the last three seasons, Mason is likely to be the primary back for some stretch of 2026.

A healthier offensive line and the addition of Kyler Murray at quarterback should push Minnesota from 26th in scoring toward the top half of the league, which would directly benefit Mason through more goal-line opportunities and more fourth-quarter running. He is one of the top handcuff options in fantasy drafts, with real standalone value even if Jones stays healthy.

Jennings spent years buried in San Francisco's slot before injuries to others gave him a bigger role, and he flashed real ability across 2024 and 2025, including a stretch of eight touchdowns in eight weeks, while gutting through a brutal list of injuries.

He signed a one-year prove-it deal with Minnesota, where he'll likely open as the third receiver but has graded better than Jordan Addison over the past three seasons and could push into two-receiver sets. New quarterback Kyler Murray‘s low average depth of target suits Jennings' underneath game more than Addison's downfield profile.

However, in the first preseason game, Addison played in the slot while Jennings lined up as the Z receiver in 11 personnel. He's an intriguing late-round target with real upside if the offense clicks and he clicks with Murray. He also has a low floor, as he could fall to fourth on the depth chart.

Okonkwo has been one of the most efficient tight ends in football on a per-route basis over four years in Tennessee, especially after the catch, but limited routes and a near-total absence near the goal line (two targets inside the 5 in four years) have kept him at TE21 each of the last three seasons.

Washington made him its second-biggest skill-position investment this offseason, handing Okonkwo Zach Ertz‘s old role in an offense where Ertz was a top-10 tight end as recently as 2024. Okonkwo is expected to see more playing time than he had in Tennessee or than Ertz had in Washington, as Okonkwo played 12 of 14 snaps in the Commanders second preseason game.

With little proven wide receiver depth beyond Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs, Okonkwo looks like a safe bet for the third-most targets on the team. That gives him a strong floor as a low-end TE2, with his TE1 upside depending mostly on how good Washington's offense is overall and whether a few more touchdowns sneak in despite his lack of size near the end zone.

Harvey entered the league with real hype as a receiving back in Sean Payton's system, but a crowded backfield kept him a fantasy non-factor until J.K. Dobbins‘ season-ending injury handed him the lead role. He produced when given volume, averaging 15.

2 PPR points per game down the stretch to rank 13th among backs, though his efficiency was poor. Harvey’s 2026 outlook is wide open: The Broncos added Jonah Coleman to a committee where playing time will follow performance.

The second-year rusher could climb into top-20 territory, especially if the often-injured Dobbins goes down again, or fade into an occasional receiving role if Coleman impresses.

Strange took over as Jacksonville's starter after outplaying Evan Engram. When healthy, he produced at a fantasy-starter level, averaging 11.1 PPR points per game over a seven-game stretch to rank 12th among tight ends.

Rookie second-round pick Nate Boerkircher was added mainly to handle blocking and free up Strange as a receiver, and the latter held up as a starter last season even with most of a talented receiver room healthy.

His ceiling is capped by that receiver depth, so a top-five finish is unlikely. But his ADP is that of a mid-range backup, making Strange a strong value with borderline-starter potential given his talent and quarterback.

Pineiro ranked fifth among kickers in fantasy points per game last season at 10.0 among those who played double-digit games. He was highly accurate at 96.6% on field goals, though that figure is likely to regress.

The good news is that the San Francisco 49ers were one of the league's most conservative teams in typical go-for-it situations, which should keep his attempt volume high.

His success will depend on the quality of the 49ers’ offense around him, which has already lost a wide receiver for the season and is dealing with other injuries in training camp.

Tucker climbed to the top of the Raiders' depth chart by attrition, finishing 38th in fantasy points last season, though his production leaned on a single monster game and he cleared 50 yards just four times.

The bull case is accuracy: As a deep threat, he was badly served by a quarterback room that ranked second-worst on deep and intermediate throws, and both Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza represent significant upgrades.

He also faces new competition in Jalen Nailor and second-year receivers Jack Bech and Dont'e Thornton Jr. The first game of the preseason suggested his role as the team's Z receiver remains secure and the second preseason game confirmed he remains the top wide receiver on the depth chart. He is a fine late-round pick with a path to being the No. 2 option behind Brock Bowers, but the depth chart could shift against him.

Aubrey has been the most reliable kicker in fantasy, finishing top three in scoring in all three of his seasons while making the Pro Bowl and All-Pro team each year.

His value is driven by Dallas' high-scoring offense, a defense that keeps games close and above all the team's willingness to attempt long field goals, an area where he has led the league three years running.

His 2026 schedule is also weather-friendly, with a dome home stadium and cold-weather road trips falling outside the winter season. Aubrey is the clear top kicker and, depending on scoring, worth taking earlier than the final round.

Shakir has been a reliable, high-volume slot receiver for one of the league's best quarterbacks, topping 70 catches in each of the last two seasons, but Buffalo has never expanded his role beyond the slot, capping his fantasy ceiling.

This year brings added risk: the team traded for DJ Moore, Joshua Palmer and Dalton Kincaid could command more targets, and a trend toward heavier personnel could cut his snaps.

He is still worth drafting as a trusted target in a great offense, but his upside is mostly as a flex or bye-week fill-in unless his role finally grows beyond 11 personnel.

Boutte spent his first three seasons in New England as a sacrificial X receiver, flashing early in 2025 with five touchdowns over the first eight weeks before a hamstring injury and an inconsistent finish.

A deep average depth of target paired with a thin target share made him hard to trust week to week. Houston should change that. Nico Collins holds the X role, pushing Boutte to Z, where the Texans' target rates are healthier and the routes are shorter.

The concern is snaps, since that role was split last season and Tank Dell is working his way back. He is a late-round dart throw who becomes a real waiver priority if he clears 75% of snaps in Week 1 or if Collins misses time.

Mevis was impressive in his limited time as the Rams' kicker, making 92.3% of his field goals and all of his extra points. He only averaged 9.

1 fantasy points per game despite kicking for one of the best offenses in the league. That’s because Los Angeles scored too many touchdowns and not enough field goals.

Mevis had a ridiculous three extra point attempts for every one field goal try. That is bound to have some regression, leading to more field goals and fewer extra points for Mevis, which should help his fantasy production.

A 2024 sixth-round pick, the 5-foot-8 receiver broke through late in his rookie year once Odell Beckham Jr. was released, then served as Miami's clear second option behind Jaylen Waddle in 2025 with Tyreek Hill out most of the season.

He caught a pass in every game but never topped five receptions or 50 yards in one, largely because he was an 11 personnel specialist who came off the field in two-receiver sets. Miami overhauled the offense this offseason with a new coordinator, a new quarterback and a handful of veteran and rookie receiver additions, leaving him as the notable holdover.

Receivers his size rarely reach fantasy relevance, but he could be the exception. Based on the first preseason game, he is due for a significant increase in playing time after playing 100% of snaps with the starters in 11, 12 and 21 personnel. This makes him a fine late round target.

Mendoza was the No. 1 overall pick and the best pure passer in his class, but several factors keep him below the typical top selection in fantasy.

He landed with a Raiders team that graded near the bottom of the league on offense, offers little of the rushing upside that fuels most recent first-round quarterbacks and ranks in the back third of recent first-rounders in PFF passing grade.

The Raiders also appear set to sit him behind Kirk Cousins to start, so he may not play much, if at all, this season. He is worth waiting on in dynasty rookie drafts and is a redraft option only in superflex.

Bates kicks for a Detroit Lions team that ranked in the top five in both PFF offensive grade and points scored last season. Even so, he finished only eighth among kickers in fantasy points.

The problem was distance. He converted just 3-of-8 attempts from 50 or more yards and 9-of-11 from 40 to 49, which dragged his overall field goal rate down to 79.4%.

Detroit brought in no competition during training camp, but it's fair to wonder how long the leash lasts if Bates misses a few early. He's fine to consider for the opening weeks, though he isn't worth more than a last-round pick.

Henry was a boom-or-bust tight end for most of his Patriots tenure. But his play stabilized once Drake Maye took over, finishing 16th and 13th in points per game the past two seasons with a genuinely higher ceiling.

The concerns for 2026 are his age, now 31, and added target competition from A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. A season-ending injury to blocking tight end Julian Hill also leaves the room thin enough that New England could add another body.

Henry profiles as a low-upside backup, best as a fill-in if a starter gets hurt or a riskier early pick busts.

Little ranked fifth among kickers in fantasy points last season, thanks to the Jacksonville Jaguars‘ high-powered offense.

His 51 extra point attempts ranked third at the position, which came at the cost of a relatively low field goal attempt total. He also made the longest kick in NFL history last season at 68 yards.

The one concern is weather. Jacksonville plays in Florida but has only two dome games this season, along with five in traditionally cold and windy cities, so his conversion rate could take a hit in a handful of spots.

McPherson is one of the top kicker options because he plays with one of the best offenses. He averaged just 8.

0 fantasy points per game last season, but that was largely down to Joe Burrow‘s injury, and a healthy Burrow should mean a better year.

McPherson still ranks behind other kickers attached to great offenses, though, because of where he plays. Three of his December games come in traditionally cold cities, which makes him harder to trust once the fantasy playoffs start.

Croskey-Merritt broke out from a buried depth-chart spot to a real role last season, flashing as a starter in Weeks 15 and 17 and finishing 16th among running backs in PPR points during the fantasy playoffs. However, Washington's offseason additions of Rachaad White, Jerome Ford and Kaytron Allen point to a crowded committee rather than an expanded role.

Croskey-Merritt’s complete lack of receiving work makes a third-down role unlikely, and Allen in particular threatens his short-yardage and goal-line touches, with a chance Allen even passes him on the depth chart.

Best case, the second-year back settles into the flex-caliber role he flashed late last season; more likely, he's a touchdown-dependent committee piece who's tough to trust weekly, making him a matchup-based streaming option beyond the 10th round rather than a player to roster for his standalone value alone.

Johnson has steadily grown into a fantasy-relevant tight end, peaking last season with 77 receptions and a 12th-place finish in points per game.

But that breakout leaned on inflated snap and target rates driven by injuries and midseason departures, and both are likely to regress.

New Orleans added Noah Fant, Oscar Delp, and currently injured first-round pass catcher Jordyn Tyson, all of which threaten his volume even if he keeps the starting job. He profiles as a fine, low-upside backup worth a late-round pick.

Boswell ranked ninth among kickers in fantasy points last season, and he notably converted 19 kicks of 40 or more yards.

He has been reliable across more than a decade with the Pittsburgh Steelers, but he has always been hampered by kicking in a cold-weather division.

The venue splits are even more extreme this year, with a league-leading 13 games in cold cities during the fantasy season and no dome matchups at all, the only team in that position. Pittsburgh's trust in him is a big reason Boswell still ranks in the top half at the position.

Corum was one of the NFL's most efficient runners last season, leading all backs in positive-grade rate and finishing near the top in yards per carry and first-down rate, and he steadily earned a bigger role as the year went on.

His snap share should hold or grow in a Rams offense expected to be among the league's best and to run even more, making Los Angeles a strong candidate to support two fantasy-relevant backs.

The catch is that Kyren Williams dominates the passing-down work, and until Corum earns receiving snaps, his ceiling stays capped. He's an efficient, early-down complement with standalone value but limited upside.

Dicker has been the most accurate kicker in NFL history, hitting 93.5% of his career field goals and at least 92% every season.

That accuracy has made him a top-four fantasy kicker in each of the past two years despite playing for an offense that consistently ranks outside the top 10 in scoring, and he is the only kicker with 38-plus makes in both seasons.

Dicker’s schedule is weather-friendly, with December road games in Las Vegas and Florida and the lone cold-weather trip coming in September. He is the clear No. 2 kicker behind Brandon Aubrey, only because he attempts fewer long kicks.

Folk has been remarkably accurate over the last three seasons, connecting on 78-of-81 field goal attempts. His 96% conversion rate is three percentage points clear of any other kicker with at least 20 attempts.

His problem from a fantasy perspective is volume, with just 29 field goal attempts and 22 extra points last season. At every other position, more talent means more opportunity, but kickers don't work that way.

Their attempts depend almost entirely on how often the offense stalls in scoring range. If the Atlanta Falcons play better than expected, he becomes a viable option.

Tagovailoa spent six seasons as Miami's starting quarterback, ranking 20th among quarterbacks in passing grade and 26th overall in fantasy thanks to almost no rushing production. He has not scored a rushing touchdown since 2021. His fantasy peak came in 2022, when he tied for ninth in fantasy points per game at 18.

4 while throwing to Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle, and he finished as a low-end QB2 in four of his six seasons with the Dolphins. Now in Atlanta, he is competing with Michael Penix Jr., who is recovering from a partially torn ACL, though Tagovailoa appears to be the favorite to open the season as the starter even if the Falcons still view Penix as their long-term answer.

Drake London and Kyle Pitts are legitimate weapons, but Kirk Cousins averaged just 14.0 fantasy points per game with that supporting cast over the final seven weeks last season, limiting Tagovailoa's upside. He should be viewed as a QB2 in superflex leagues, and only while he holds the starting job.

Myers led all kickers in fantasy points last season with 202. He attempted 48 field goals, tied for the league lead, and 48 extra points, tied for fifth.

Seattle should remain one of the best offenses in the NFL, which keeps him in range of a top-few finish at the position.

The main concern is the outdoor home stadium, as many of the other top kickers play in domes. Only two of Seattle's games this season come in a dome or under a retractable roof, and neither falls in December.

Sadiq was the only tight end drafted in the top 50 this year, a lighter, receiving-oriented prospect in the mold of Brock Bowers, Colston Loveland, Kyle Pitts and Dalton Kincaid.

He matches that group's elite athleticism but not their college production, with a career receiving grade well below theirs, in part because he spent two seasons behind Terrance Ferguson at Oregon.

He lands with a Jets team that already has young pass catchers in Mason Taylor and Omar Cooper Jr., so opportunities will be shared, though he has a realistic shot at second on the team in targets. That makes him a late-round redraft option at best, but a worthwhile first-round pick in dynasty rookie drafts.

On one hand, Bass kicks for a Buffalo Bills team that has consistently fielded one of the best offenses in the league.

On the other, he missed all of last season with a lower-body injury. Buffalo also plays most of its games outdoors in chilly cities, including four of five in December.

He is a better option than plenty of kickers on worse offenses, but he isn't someone you can trust in a starting lineup every week.

Loop was an effective kicker, though the Baltimore Ravens rarely sent him out for long attempts.

He averaged just 8.5 fantasy points per game last season, largely a reflection of the offense around him.

Baltimore should be better with a healthier Lamar Jackson, which should put Loop among the league leaders in either field goal or extra point attempts.

Jones has been one of the most efficient runners in NFL history, but his production has slipped in Minnesota, with career-low grades in 2024 and a further step back in 2025 amid injuries and added competition.

A hamstring and a hip injury cost him significant time, and Jordan Mason, who graded notably better as a runner, cut into his workload.

Now the second-oldest halfback likely to make a roster, Jones faces a real threat to his volume from both Mason and rookie Demond Claiborne. His range spans a bounce-back starter with RB2 value to a diminished piece in a committee.

Butker averaged 8.8 fantasy points per game last season, right at league average for a starter and just outside the range worth using weekly.

A big part of the problem was the Kansas City Chiefs‘ offense, which should improve this season with Kenneth Walker III at running back. That cuts both ways, though, since a better offense often means more extra points and fewer field goals.

He also still kicks in a stadium that produces cold, windy games. Butker belongs in fantasy lineups when the matchup and situation line up, not as a set-and-forget option.

Nailor held down a No. 3 role in Minnesota for two seasons and out-graded Jordan Addison last year, and he now projects as a starter in Las Vegas opposite Tre Tucker in an offense adding Klint Kubiak, Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza.

His profile fits what Mendoza does best, and his grades have been the stronger of the pair.

The concern is that he sat behind the first team in the second preseason game while Tucker rested, and Malik Benson and Noah Brown are both in the mix behind him. He is a late-round dart throw in deeper leagues who should be drafted after Tucker.

Dulcich flashed real ability as a 2022 third-round rookie, but hamstring injuries wrecked his first two seasons and pushed him off the Broncos and Giants rosters before Miami claimed him. He found a role with the Dolphins down the stretch in 2025, ranking third among tight ends at 2.

31 yards per route run and leading the position on second and third downs despite never topping 60% of the snaps. Miami then cleared the decks around him, moving on from Darren Waller, Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle while adding only cheap rookies and free agents, and the new front office has openly tabbed him as a breakout candidate.

Dulcich is now a favorite to lead the team in targets, giving him a high floor, with his ceiling tied mostly to how many touchdowns a rebuilding Dolphins offense can produce.

Elliott has spent the last nine seasons as the Philadelphia Eagles‘ kicker, scoring at least 130 points in three of four years from 2021 to 2024.

The offense had a down year in 2025, and a bounce back would put him back in fantasy starter range. The concern is distance, as he has converted just 33% of his attempts beyond 50 yards over the last two seasons.

Elliott’s contract means the job is safe, but Philadelphia may be reluctant to send him out from 50-plus, which caps his ceiling.

Monangai was a 2025 seventh-round pick who quickly climbed to the No. 2 role behind D'Andre Swift, settling into regular double-digit-carry usage after Week 5 and producing 10.4 PPR points per game from Week 6 on, good for 30th among running backs.

With no real roster additions to challenge the pecking order, a similar split looks likely, since Swift graded clearly better last season as a runner, receiver and pass-blocker. He hyperextended his knee and might not be ready for Week 1.

Monangai's appeal depends heavily on league format: In shallower leagues with only 20 to 24 weekly starters, he's mostly a handcuff with little standalone value, but in leagues running 28 to 36 starters, his floor makes him a usable weekly option.

Addison has been a productive second option opposite Justin Jefferson, but his fantasy value has leaned heavily on touchdowns and on playing with accurate deep-ball quarterbacks, since he is a rare small receiver who wins downfield.

Shaky quarterback play tanked him last season, dropping him to 48th in points per game, and this year's upgrade to Kyler Murray under center still isn't a strong deep passer. He has Kyler Murray, who has a history of shorter passes.

Addison played in the slot in 11 personnel in the Vikings first preseason game, suggesting Addison might see more short passes. He is a risky flex option, depending on how much trust Murray gains in Addison.

McLaughlin finished seventh among kickers in fantasy points last season despite the Tampa Bay Buccaneers‘ struggles on offense and a relatively low 84.

2% field goal rate. The good news is that he tied for the league lead with 11 makes from 50 or more yards. Playing in Florida helps as well.

Only three games on Tampa Bay's schedule come in outdoor venues in traditionally cold cities, and just one of those falls in December.

Smack is a sixth-round rookie and currently the only kicker on the Green Bay Packers‘ roster after the team carried three earlier in the offseason.

He lands on an offense that ranked eighth in team grade last season at 81.1, but he is at a disadvantage relative to other kickers on good teams because of where he plays.

Green Bay has 11 games in cold, outdoor stadiums, and the fantasy season closes with three matchups at home, plus a trip to Chicago.

Santos kicks for a Chicago Bears offense that ranked in the top 10 in both points scored and PFF offensive grade last season.

That combination usually puts a kicker inside the top 10 in fantasy points as well. The problem is the venue. He converted just 83.

3% of his field goals last season while playing in one of the toughest stadiums in the league to kick, and Chicago has only two dome games on the schedule this year, none of them in December.

Fairbairn ranked second among kickers in fantasy points last season, but he is due for regression. He tied for the league lead in field goal attempts while ranking just 23rd in extra points.

The Houston Texans should score more touchdowns and settle for fewer field goals this year, which would bring those totals down. The venue situation cuts against him too.

Houston plays indoors, which has helped him in the past, but the December slate includes road trips to Pittsburgh, Washington, Philadelphia and Green Bay.

Reichard earned a 93.8 PFF kicking grade last season, second-best at the position behind Brandon Aubrey. He tied for the league lead with 11 makes from 50 or more yards and converted an impressive 94.3% overall despite that heavy long-range workload.

The problem was that the Minnesota Vikings‘ offense wasn't scoring enough. If Minnesota takes a real step forward with Kyler Murray at quarterback, he can be a weekly fantasy starter, but that possibility doesn't make Reichard worth taking over kickers already attached to great offenses.

The dome helps, though it's worth noting that two of the Vikings' December games are outdoors in the Northeast.

Douglas went 75th overall to Miami without much college production, but the measurables are excellent and the fit is unusually clean. He will start the season as Miami's X receiver and new coordinator Bobby Slowik has developed productive X receivers before.

Douglas played 100% of snaps with the starters in their first preseason game, and only played the first drive in the second, giving Douglas a chance to lead the team in targets.

Fellow rookie Chris Bell is on the non-football injury list, but there is a chance once Bell is healthy, he could take playing time from Douglas. He is a late round target, who will likely be moving up ADP slowly but surely.

Borregales has the classic problem of kicking for a potent offense in a cold-weather city, in a division with two more outdoor cold-weather teams.

Twelve of the New England Patriots‘ 16 games during the fantasy season come in traditional cold cities, including all five in December.

He can likely be trusted early on, but he becomes a drop candidate as the year goes on.

Whoever wins the Indianapolis Colts‘ kicking competition should be a fantasy starter more often than not. Among teams that play in domes or under a retractable roof, Indianapolis ranked in the top four in both PFF offensive grade at 80.

7 and points scored at 466. The complication is that the job is genuinely open, with Grupe facing competition from Spencer Shrader.

Grupe made all 11 field goals and 10 extra points across his five games with Indianapolis to close the season. Anyone planning to skip a kicker in the draft and add one before Week 1 would be smart to target whoever wins here.

Lutz has spent the last three seasons as the Denver Broncos‘ kicker. He should benefit from a good offense, and the altitude is a real edge for kickers in Denver, but it's one he barely uses.

Altitude pays off most on long attempts, and he has never been one to take many. Lutz has 47 tries from 50 or more yards across 148 career games and converted only 29 of them.

Last season, 21 of his 28 makes came from inside 40 yards. He is a dependable but limited option, best streamed in weeks when Denver is expected to score more than usual.

Zvada is an undrafted rookie out of Michigan who appears to be the favorite for the New York Giants‘ kicking job.

New York finished in the bottom half of the league in both PFF offensive grade and points scored last season. The Giants play outdoors in a cold city, though five of their games come in domes or under a retractable roof.

If the New York offense is healthier and more productive this year, there should be weeks where Zvada is worth starting.

Barner locked down Seattle's starting tight end job as a rookie and graded 12th at the position, showing borderline-starter talent at just 24.

He also carries a sneaky touchdown path, converting 10-of-11 short-yardage direct-snap carries, and could see goal-line work early with Zach Charbonnet sidelined.

The problem is volume: Seattle is run-heavy, Jaxon Smith-Njigba commands the targets and Rashid Shaheed, the running backs and rookie Elijah Arroyo all have claims on the rest, leaving Barner with one of the lowest target rates at the position. He is a high-risk, high-upside late-round backup best paired with a safe starter.

Hockenson was a perennial top-six fantasy tight end before a torn ACL and MCL at the end of 2023, and he hasn't been the same since, declining in receptions, yards and grade across the two seasons after.

Some of last year's drop may trace to poor quarterback play, given how sharply his average depth of target and target rate fell.

He now catches passes from Kyler Murray, who has historically supported productive tight ends, offering a bounce-back path if Hockenson is finally fully recovered. The risk is that he never regains his old form, or that added competition like Jauan Jennings caps his target share.

Schultz set a career high with 82 receptions last season and finished 13th in fantasy points per game, though that came with Tank Dell out, Stefon Diggs gone and most of the tight end room injured.

Houston has since added Foster Moreau and drafted Marlin Klein, which points to more two-tight-end sets and some risk to his snap count.

Working the other way, Jayden Higgins‘ season-ending ACL tear leaves Schultz as the No. 2 target earner on the roster, and he sat out the second preseason game while the other tight ends rotated. He is a safe TE2 with a path to TE1 production if nobody behind him emerges.

Fitzgerald won the Carolina Panthers‘ kicking job last season as an undrafted rookie. He was fine from short range but made only two of five attempts beyond 50 yards, so long-range volume isn't likely to be part of his profile.

That, combined with the offense around him, makes him one of the last starting kickers to consider in drafts.

He does have the job to himself, though, and Carolina showed some willingness to kick in situations where most teams go for it on fourth down. That's enough to move him up a few spots in the rankings.

Szmyt won the Cleveland Browns‘ kicking job in 2025 after a strong UFL season in 2024 and a late-season signing to Cleveland's practice squad. He was solid as a rookie starter, converting 88.

9% of his field-goal attempts and 96.2% of his extra points despite the wind he kicks in. His problem is the offense, which posted the league's lowest team grade last season at 57.0.

Some improvement is expected, but the top half of the league is a stretch. All five December games are outdoors in cold-weather cities as well. He is a kicker to avoid outside of 32-team leagues.

Smyth is a Northern Ireland native who appeared in six games for the New Orleans Saints last season. He converted just 75% of his field-goal attempts but was perfect inside 40 yards, extra points included.

He holds a slight edge over Tanner Brown for the job. Any kicker in an open competition is hard to trust in drafts, especially one attached to an offense that scored only 306 points last year.

He still ranks ahead of a few others, though, because New Orleans plays in a dome and has no cold-weather games in December.

Gay has been a journeyman kicker who hasn't reached an 84% field goal rate in any of the last three seasons. He played 10 games for the Washington Commanders and two for the San Francisco 49ers last year.

The Las Vegas Raiders signed him to a one-year deal, and he is competing with international player Kansei Matsuzawa.

He has the benefit of a domed stadium, but he needs both a better offense in front of him and better accuracy of his own to belong in fantasy lineups.

Slye managed just 8.4 fantasy points per game last season, a function of the Tennessee Titans‘ offense giving him only 35 field goal attempts and 27 extra points.

If the offense grows, he is in a good spot, because the schedule works in Slye’s favor.

Tennessee plays outdoors, but none of its December games come in cold-weather cities.

White was a featured back in Tampa before losing his role to Bucky Irving. He's since built his reputation as one of the league's better receiving backs, ranking fifth in yards after the catch over the last three seasons.

He signed a modest one-year deal with Washington into a heavy committee with Jerome Ford, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, Jeremy McNichols and Kaytron Allen. While strong practices have White positioned for the most secure role, that looks like Austin Ekeler‘s old third-down job rather than a true workhorse spot.

The likeliest outcome is a passing-game share similar to Ekeler's 2024, when Ekeler finished 29th in PPR points per game on a good Washington offense. That makes White a fine, safe RB3 rather than a player worth reaching for.

McMillan displayed intrigue as a newcomer with a huge late-season stretch, scoring seven touchdowns in the final five games, but a scary preseason neck injury wiped out most of his 2025.

He returns to a crowded Tampa Bay room where Emeka Egbuka and Chris Godwin are the likely top two, though his talent gives him a path to push Godwin or step up if injuries hit.

With Mike Evans gone and Baker Mayfield expected to bounce back, the offense should support two fantasy-relevant receivers. McMillan is a fine end-of-draft pick, especially if camp news points to a bigger role.

Mitchell was a talented early-round pick who couldn't crack Indianapolis' lineup, stuck behind a career-best stretch from Alec Pierce and undone by a costly Week 4 audition before a midseason trade to the Jets.

He flashed there as the top target while Garrett Wilson was hurt, and New York plans to keep him as its X receiver, though he now shares a room with a healthy Wilson and rookie Omar Cooper Jr. under new coordinator Frank Reich and quarterback Geno Smith.

He is worth a late-round pick as a high-pedigree receiver finally getting a real shot to start.

Vele has been a productive role player across two seasons, clearing a 70.0 receiving grade in both despite bouncing between depth chart spots in Denver and New Orleans, and he was starting for the Saints last season before a shoulder injury ended his year.

First-round pick Jordyn Tyson had pushed him back to third on the depth chart, but Tyson's right hamstring injury is expected to cost him up to two months.

That should install Vele as the second receiver for roughly the first six weeks. He is a worthwhile late-round pick for anyone who drafted rookies or injured receivers and needs a bridge to start the season.

Freiermuth was a reliable, touchdown-scoring tight end who finished 13th at the position as recently as 2024, but his value plummeted in 2025 when Pittsburgh added Jonnu Smith and gave Darnell Washington a bigger role, cutting his snaps to just 50.6%.

Both Jonnu Smith and coordinator Arthur Smith are now gone under new head coach Mike McCarthy, which should open up more playing time. However, he played less than 50% of snaps with the starters in the Steelers' first preseason game, suggesting he won't see a substantial increase in playing time.

The risks are a PFF receiving grade that has slipped over the past three seasons and added target competition from Michael Pittman Jr. and rookie Germie Bernard. He's a fine late-round gamble on your backup, with a chance to return to borderline-starter value.

Patterson was competing with Zane Gonzalez for Miami’s kicking job, but Gonzalez landed on injured reserve, leaving Patterson as the last man standing.

Patterson kicked for Miami last season but has attempted just 13 field goals beyond 50 yards in 61 career games, a sign that teams haven't trusted him from that range.

The combination of the long-range concerns, concerns around Miami’s offense, and the possibility that Miami brings in more competition makes Patterson a kicker to avoid.

Ryland is entering his third season as the Arizona Cardinals‘ kicker. He managed just 7.6 fantasy points per game last year, fourth-lowest among kickers expected to hold a lead job this season.

The problem was a combination of the offense in front of him and a low 75.8% field goal rate. The accuracy should bounce back, but expectations aren't high for Arizona either.

He is a kicker to avoid, though if the offense outperforms, the retractable roof and a December schedule free of cold-weather games work in his favor.

Tyson went eighth overall as the second wide receiver off the board in the 2026 draft, and top-10 receivers have historically produced fantasy value even as rookies.

New Orleans is not an ideal landing spot given Tyler Shough‘s middling quarterback play and a Saints offense that scored the fifth-fewest points last season, but Chris Olave‘s target volume and modest PFF receiving grade leave room for Tyson to carve out a significant role early.

If he overtakes Olave as the top option, he immediately pays off; if not, he profiles as a borderline top-40 receiver in a below-average offense. Tyson's hamstring injury that will likely leave him on injured reserve to start the season also complicates his fantasy potential as a rookie.

Ridley has been a boom-or-bust producer for Tennessee, capable of long dominant stretches but also periods as a complete non-factor, and injuries have limited him to two full seasons in the past five.

Now 31 and coming off a hamstring injury and fibula fracture, he faces steep new target competition from fourth overall pick Carnell Tate and free-agent addition Wan'Dale Robinson, leaving him projected third in targets.

A third receiver in this offense holds little fantasy value on paper. Ridley’s case rests on the offense improving under a new coordinator and a second-year Cam Ward, with a chance he remains the top outside option early.

A fourth-round pick in 2025, Helm won the second tight end job immediately and grew into a larger role as his rookie year went on, topping 55% of snaps six times over the final eight weeks after doing so once in the first 10. He posted a 69.3 receiving grade, 17th among tight ends with at least 50 targets, though his 3.

7 yards after the catch per reception was among the worst in that group. Tennessee overhauled the offense this offseason with Brian Daboll taking over as coordinator, Chig Okonkwo leaving in free agency and Daniel Bellinger following Daboll from New York as the main competition.

He should be the top receiving tight end, but with Carnell Tate and Wan'Dale Robinson added at wide receiver, he is a deeper-league option best suited to managers drafting for upside.

Flournoy was a sixth-round pick in 2024 who played sparingly as a rookie and opened 2025 fifth on the depth chart. Early injuries pushed him past 50% of snaps in Week 5, where he caught six passes for 114 yards, and he held roughly 40% to 45% of snaps even once the room got healthy, including a nine-catch, 115-yard, one-touchdown game against the Detroit Lions in Week 14 with everyone available.

His 80.3 PFF grade would usually make him a second option, but CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens lock him into the third spot in an offense that ranked sixth in 11 personnel last season and could lead the league in it this year.

He will likely go undrafted in redraft, since other third receivers have clearer paths up their depth charts, but he is worth rostering in deeper and best ball leagues for the handful of big games. If Lamb or Pickens misses extended time, Flournoy would be one of the top waiver targets of the year.

Otton has played at least 92% of offensive snaps in each of the last three seasons and just signed a three-year, $30 million deal, so the playing time is secure.

The production is not, because it has swung almost entirely on health elsewhere: over the last two years he averaged 13.2 PPR points per game in the nine contests Mike Evans and Chris Godwin both missed or barely played, and 7.0 in every other game.

New offensive coordinator Zac Robinson is a real point of optimism after what he did with Kyle Pitts, but Evans' departure leaves a deep young receiver group around Godwin rather than a thin one. Leave him on the waiver wire and monitor the receiver injury report.

Gesicki finished 13th among tight ends in 2024 on the strength of five big games, three of which came with Tee Higgins out, but he also had nine games with 2 or fewer yards or three or fewer receptions.

The 2025 season was worse, with nothing over 20 yards through five weeks, a pectoral strain costing him the middle stretch, and no real spike even when Higgins missed time again.

Cincinnati rotates its tight ends heavily, so he is not guaranteed 12 personnel or third-down work, and Erick All‘s return could cut into the snaps further. He belongs on the waiver wire, though the Joe Burrow connection and the proven ceiling keep him ahead of a few other starting tight ends.

Jeudy's Cleveland production has swung entirely on quarterback play, thriving with Jameis Winston and cratering with everyone else, and Winston is now a Giants backup.

With Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders as the likely starters, his efficiency projects poorly, and the Browns added K.C. Concepcion, Denzel Boston and a bigger role for Isaiah Bond, crowding his target share.

The counterargument is alignment: Jeudy was miscast at X last season and grades far better off the line, and the rookies could push him back to Z while drawing coverage away from him. He's a late-round deep-league flier who could be a weekly starter if the pieces fit, but is droppable within a month or two if they don't.

Allen is 13th all time in receptions and was a fixture in fantasy lineups for most of the last decade, but the last two seasons have brought him down to the WR35-to-WR40 range and, in 2025, a part-time role that pulled him out of the slot.

He signed with the Indianapolis Colts in the middle of training camp, reuniting with head coach Shane Steichen, who was his offensive coordinator during one of his better statistical seasons.

He should open at Z in three-receiver sets, though Josh Downs is the likelier option in heavier packages. A low-end WR3 outcome is his realistic ceiling, and reaching it means taking targets from teammates who are already established there.

Charbonnet has showcased clear fantasy upside, excelling as a starter during Kenneth Walker III‘s 2024 absence and scoring 12 rushing touchdowns as the goal-line back in 2025, though a committee split constricted his value.

He tore his ACL in the playoffs and opened camp on the PUP list, so he is likely to miss the start of the season. The encouraging sign is that he was working off to the side during OTAs and has been tracking ahead of schedule, which points more toward a few missed weeks than half a season.

With Walker gone, Charbonnet’s competition is now Jadarian Price, George Holani and Emanuel Wilson. Charbonnet’s upside is an early return to full form and a bigger role, but the likelier outcome is diminished effectiveness for much of the year and a role similar to last season's.

The Texans finished as the second-best fantasy defense last season and return largely the same lineup, with safety Reed Blankenship as the only notable addition.

Some regression is likely, since a league-leading four defensive touchdowns plus top-five marks in fumble recoveries and interceptions all come from volatile areas.

The Texans’ standing in the more stable categories is reassuring, though, as Houston ranked second in points allowed and first in yards surrendered. They should be a top fantasy defense again in 2026, with luck determining whether they are the No. 1 unit or closer to fifth.

Harris quietly carved out a real role as a rookie, playing 86.6% of the Chargers' single-receiver snaps from Week 7 on and cutting into two-receiver work by midseason.

With Keenan Allen unsigned, he could lead all Los Angeles receivers in playing time, though the production has not caught up yet, with a 66.6 PFF receiving grade and a best game of four catches for 54 yards.

The complication is new coordinator Mike McDaniel, whose speed-based system may not fit a receiver who lacks the burst of his teammates. Harris is a speculative late-round pick in deeper leagues, with the first month of the season likely to settle whether the role and scheme work.

The Rams ranked fifth in fantasy defense last season and were well-rounded across the board, finishing top 10 in points allowed, interceptions, sacks and fumble recoveries.

They got significantly better this offseason, trading for Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie and signing Jaylen Watson, all upgrades over the players they lost.

A rumored Aaron Donald return could raise the ceiling even higher. The main concern is one of the league's toughest schedules, but this should still be a strong fantasy defense.

The 46th overall pick in 2025 barely played through five weeks, then earned a steadily larger role, finishing with 73.1% of snaps from Weeks 14-17 while handling 80% of third-down 11 personnel and every 13 personnel snap.

He caught only 11 passes but averaged 21.0 yards per reception with three touchdowns, and Sean McVay has since talked him up as a player who can line up anywhere on the offense. The concern is that his 18.

3 average depth of target was more than six yards higher than any other tight end, so the volume depends on the Rams mixing in easier throws, and Los Angeles returns all three of its other tight ends plus a second-round rookie. He is a late-round pick in deeper leagues with a real chance to become a waiver wire target after one big week.

The real reason for optimism is youth. Eleven of the top 15 players on the depth chart are 27 or younger, so most of this group should improve rather than decline.

However, there is concern around Micah Parsons, who is expected to start the season on the PUP list.

Ideally, he will be fully healthy by midseason, but there is no guarantee.

Mitchell flashed elite potential as a rookie with the Ravens, averaging 8.4 yards per carry over a six-week stretch before an ACL injury derailed his development. He arrives in Los Angeles with the highest PFF grade of the Chargers' three-back room over the past three seasons despite his down 2024 campaign.

The key factor is his fit with new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who brought Mitchell to Los Angeles himself, while Omarion Hampton and Kimani Vidal are holdovers.

Mitchell shares the same rare size-speed profile as McDaniel's previous featured back De'Von Achane, with both sitting at 5-foot-8 or shorter and 200 pounds or lighter while posting sub-4.40 40-yard dash times. If McDaniel ultimately prefers Mitchell over his other options, the upside is top-10 at the position.

Rodriguez has been buried on the depth chart for most of his career but has been quietly one of the most efficient runners in the league, ranking near the top in yards after contact, first-down rate and PFF rushing grade over the past three seasons.

The catch is he boasts almost no receiving usage, with just six career catches, and he now joins a crowded Jacksonville backfield alongside Bhayshul Tuten and LeQuint Allen.

Tuten is the likeliest to lead the group in fantasy points given his dual-threat role, but Rodriguez's efficiency and bigger frame could earn him goal-line work in a potentially high-scoring offense. That makes him an intriguing late-round option, especially if the Jacksonville offense supports two relevant backs.

The Lions allowed 413 points last season to rank 22nd in the league, but they were better than that in fantasy thanks to a pass rush led by Aidan Hutchinson that produced 49 sacks, tied for fourth-most.

Detroit lost real production in the front seven, with Alex Anzalone, DJ Reader, Roy Lopez and Al-Quadin Muhammad all playing at least 400 snaps and grading above 67.0 before departing. D.J.

Wonnum and second-round pick Derrick Moore are the key additions, but the bounce-back case rests mostly on returning players — including safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, who both failed to finish last season.

The Bengals yielded the third-most points and second-most yards in the league last season, though 13 interceptions kept them respectable in fantasy.

Trey Hendrickson‘s departure is the biggest loss, but he missed most of last season anyway, and the three other players gone with at least 300 snaps all graded at 64.0 or worse.

Cincinnati then went shopping, adding Dexter Lawrence II, Boye Mafe and Bryan Cook, who may now be the three best players on the defense. With a young roster around them, the Bengals should improve, and there's a path to an above-average unit if the younger players develop.

Hunter was establishing a role as Jacksonville's third receiver with upside, including a 101-yard, one-touchdown game in Week 7, before an LCL tear ended his rookie season.

His path back to fantasy relevance is now much harder, with Jakobi Meyers acquired via trade and Parker Washington thriving in his old role, likely leaving Hunter fourth on the depth chart.

Jacksonville also drafted two tight ends, pointing toward more two-tight-end sets that would cut into his snaps, while the departure of Greg Newsome II could pull him further toward defense. Hunter profiles as a part-time offensive player with unpredictable spike weeks, though the talent that made him the No. 2 pick keeps a breakout in play.

Stribling was a surprise pick at 33rd overall, a physical 6-foot-2 receiver who wins at the catch point more than through separation.

He is behind Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel and Demarcus Robinson to start, but all three are past 30 and two have injury histories, and he has already out-snapped them in the slot through two preseason games while producing at both alignments.

His long-term role is at X once Evans moves on. He is worth a late-round pick as a receiver who should play meaningful snaps immediately with real upside beyond that.

The Eagles ranked fifth in points allowed last season but only seventh in fantasy points, held back by a lack of big plays and a sack total that fell outside the top 10, much like their 2024 finish.

They reshaped the secondary this offseason, moving on from Adoree' Jackson and Reed Blankenship while adding cornerback Riq Woolen.

Philadelphia’s biggest boost is edge rusher Jonathan Greenard, who should start and help generate more pressure. The changes should keep the Eagles among the top 10 fantasy defenses, and while the upside is capped, the floor is very safe.

New England allowed the fourth-fewest points in the league last season but was only a borderline top-10 fantasy defense, generating five combined defensive and special teams touchdowns while ranking seventh-worst in sacks.

Recovering as many fumbles as the Patriots forced points toward regression, and the roster churn doesn't help. Indeed, 10 defenders who played at least 100 snaps are gone, including starters K'Lavon Chaisson, Jack Gibbens and Jaylinn Hawkins.

Kevin Byard III headlines the additions but turns 33 this year, and edge rushers Dre'Mont Jones and Harold Landry III both grade below 70.0 as pass-rushers over the past three seasons. Treat the Patriots as a situational start, with mild regression likely.

Sampson showcased strong receiving ability as a rookie, ranking second among running backs in yards per route run at 1.86, just behind Bijan Robinson. However, his rushing efficiency was held back by an offensive line that gave him just 0.

3 yards before contact per carry, tied for the second-lowest mark by any back with at least 50 carries over the last 20 years. Cleveland overhauled that line this offseason, adding Spencer Fano, Tytus Howard, Zion Johnson and Elgton Jenkins, and Jerome Ford‘s departure without a meaningful replacement should push Sampson into a significantly larger role.

If Quinshon Judkins is fully healthy, Sampson profiles as a high-upside flex with standalone value thanks to his receiving ability. If Judkins misses time following his Week 16 dislocated ankle and fractured fibula, Sampson becomes a likely must-start.

The Steelers ranked ninth among fantasy defenses last season, generating big plays across the board with top-three marks in fumble recoveries and defensive touchdowns and top-10 finishes in sacks and interceptions, even while allowing slightly more points than league average.

The front seven returns largely intact, and the secondary was rebuilt after five defensive backs with at least 100 snaps departed, with Jamel Dean and Jaquan Brisker headlining the replacements.

Dean should be an upgrade after posting an 80.7 overall PFF grade in Tampa Bay. Pittsburgh figures to remain a top-10 fantasy defense, though the age of core pieces like T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey is a real risk.

The Ravens have long been a strong team defense, ranking second as recently as 2023. Although the past two seasons have been quieter, they finished 2025 strong by scoring the eighth-most fantasy points among defenses over the final eight weeks.

The big reason to expect a leap in 2026 is the front four, headlined by the addition of Trey Hendrickson, this offseason's top free agent and the owner of the fifth-best PFF pass-rush grade among edge defenders over the past three seasons.

With Calais Campbell back, a possible return from Nnamdi Madubuike and stars like Kyle Hamilton and Roquan Smith already in place, Baltimore should field an excellent defense against a favorable schedule.

The Chiefs allowed the sixth-fewest points in the league last season at 328, yet finished as just the 22nd-ranked fantasy defense because they never made big plays, forcing a league-low six fumbles, scoring no touchdowns or safeties and recording a below-average 35 sacks.

The offseason brought heavy turnover, with Jaylen Watson, Bryan Cook and Trent McDuffie all departing after grading at 74.0 or better, along with five front-seven players who logged at least 300 snaps.

Kansas City leaned on the draft to replace them, taking three defenders inside the first 40 picks. More big plays would lift the fantasy outlook, but this is a matchup-based streamer rather than a weekly starter.

The Jaguars finished third in fantasy points last season, powered by four defensive and special teams touchdowns and 22 interceptions, the second-most in the league.

Jacksonville then lost two starters in linebacker Devin Lloyd, who took his 87.9 overall grade to Carolina, and safety Andrew Wingard, who signed with Arizona, while adding nothing notable in free agency beyond minor defensive line depth.

A small step back is likely, though a healthy Travis Hunter playing a bigger defensive role helps offset it. Treat Jacksonville as a matchup-based start rather than a weekly one.

The Broncos were the fourth-ranked fantasy defense last season, powered by a league-leading 68 sacks and the third-fewest points allowed behind a front four led by Nik Bonitto and Zach Allen.

The unit returns largely intact, losing John Franklin-Myers and Dre Greenlaw while adding only third-round lineman Tyler Onyedim.

Some sack regression is likely, but Denver should stay among the league's best defenses, and one of the top fantasy defenses as a result.

The Bills were a middling fantasy defense last season, concluding the year above-average in points allowed but generating fewer big plays than a typical unit.

Buffalo let an aging group walk, with nine players who logged at least 200 snaps now unsigned, including Joey Bosa and DaQuan Jones, and none of their free-agent additions graded above 60.0 last season. The plan is clearly youth, with both second-round picks spent on defense in edge rusher T.J.

Parker and cornerback Davison Igbinosun, plus a 2025 class in which Maxwell Hairston, T.J. Sanders and Landon Jackson all topped 500 snaps as rookies. Avoid the Bills early until those young players prove themselves, but the upside is real if the drafting hits.

San Francisco finished with the seventh-worst fantasy defense last season, undone by a league-low 20 sacks despite slightly above-average points allowed.

The rebound case starts with health, as Nick Bosa, Fred Warner and free-agent addition Dre Greenlaw are the three highest-graded 49ers over the past three seasons, and none topped 400 snaps last year.

Five players with at least 500 snaps are gone, with Miami defensive backs Jack Jones and Ashtyn Davis among the veteran replacements. The other swing factor is youth, with six defenders drafted in the first four rounds of 2024 and 2025 in line for big roles, none of whom carries a career PFF grade above 64.0 yet.

The Seahawks were the clear No. 1 fantasy defense last season, averaging nearly a point more than the second-place unit while leading the league in points allowed.

Some pullback is coming, as their seven combined defensive and special teams touchdowns are likely to regress. Also, free agency thinned their depth with safety Coby Bryant, cornerback Riq Woolen and defensive end Boye Mafe all departing.

A bottom-five schedule adds to the headwinds. Between the touchdown regression, the personnel losses and the tougher slate, Seattle should slide from last season's total but still lands as a top-five defense.

Marks took over as both the receiving and lead-rushing back in Houston as a rookie, but the run game struggled behind a still-shaky offensive line, and he graded far better as a receiver than a runner.

The Texans traded for David Montgomery this offseason, and it has been clear he'll lead a one-two punch, likely pushing Marks into more of a passing-down role that should suit him better.

That limits his standalone fantasy value to very deep leagues where a near-even split gives him flex appeal. His main value is as Houston's clear handcuff, a role that could mirror his second-half production last season, when he ranked 32nd in points from Weeks 10 to 18.

Cleveland finished as the eighth-ranked fantasy defense last season on the strength of 53 sacks — which ranked third — and four defensive touchdowns — tied for the league lead — while grading out as average in most other categories.

The problem is that both of the Browns’ best players are gone, with Myles Garrett (93.0) traded to the Rams and Devin Bush (87.6) signing with Chicago, leaving no returning defender who graded above 80.0.

Jared Verse came back in the Garrett trade, and his 82.2 overall PFF grade makes him the new centerpiece, with Quincy Williams added from the Jets after an injury-shortened 2025. Expect a below-average unit that is only worth streaming in favorable matchups.

The Giants were the fifth-worst fantasy defense last season and reshaped the roster accordingly, trading Dexter Lawrence II for a first-round pick while losing Bobby Okereke, Cor'Dale Flott and Dane Belton, all of whom played more than 700 snaps.

New York brought in 16 players who took a snap elsewhere last season, though only a handful matter. That group is led by defensive tackle DJ Reader, plus fifth overall pick Arvell Reese.

Reese is slated to start immediately, but rookie linebackers rarely transform a defense, and replacing Lawrence with Reader looks more like a downgrade than an upgrade. There isn't much reason to expect a significantly better unit this season.

The Colts were the definition of an average fantasy defense last season, and they responded with a near-total overhaul, as 19 players who took a defensive snap in Indianapolis are no longer on the roster.

That group includes starters Kwity Paye, Zaire Franklin and Nick Cross, all of whom graded below 60.0, plus longtime nickel Kenny Moore II. The replacements are underwhelming on paper, with eight veteran additions who all graded under a 64.

0 and rookies CJ Allen and AJ Haulcy both in line to start. The real reason for optimism is a full season of Sauce Gardner after a midseason trade netted just two full games before injury, though average is still the likeliest outcome.

Spears was promising in 2023 but has since been slowed by a string of injuries, including two concussions and a high ankle sprain, and his efficiency dipped last season.

He returns to a familiar timeshare with Tony Pollard, who has outgraded him as a rusher while Spears has been the better receiver. A new coaching staff, including hot-hand-friendly coordinator Brian Daboll, adds uncertainty that could reshape the rotation.

Spears out-snapped Pollard in the first two preseason games, suggesting he will have a legitimate opportunity to become the lead back. This makes him an intriguing late round pick.

The Jets scored the fewest fantasy points of any defense last season at 47.0, a full 12 behind the second-worst, and they traded away their two best players in Quinnen Williams and Sauce Gardner at midseason.

New York then overhauled the roster, letting eight veterans who all graded below 64.0 walk while adding eight players with at least 380 snaps last season, headlined by T'Vondre Sweat, David Onyemata, Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick, who each graded at 79.0 or better.

The draft brought more help, with edge rusher David Bailey going second overall and cornerback D'Angelo Ponds in the second round. Last season's numbers mean almost nothing here, and while a below-average unit is the reasonable expectation, the range of outcomes is unusually wide.

Pacheco was a productive starter in Kansas City before a fractured fibula in 2024 derailed him, and his PFF grades have dipped notably in the two seasons since. He joins Detroit on a modest deal to replace David Montgomery as Jahmyr Gibbs‘ backup in a role that's been shrinking and produced modest fantasy returns even for Montgomery last season.

Pacheco's added size could carve out some goal-line work, giving him flex appeal in deeper or multi-flex leagues, and his main value is as a handcuff who could become the feature back if Gibbs gets hurt.

That outcome isn't guaranteed, though, since Sione Vaki is a real threat to win the backup job outright in camp and Pacheco is dealing with a sprained MCL which will hold him out for the rest of preseason.

Dallas was the second-worst fantasy defense last season, allowing the most points and third-most yards in the league, and 10 players with at least 200 snaps are already gone.
