The rebuild was aggressive, starting with first-round picks Caleb Downs at No. 11 and Malachi Lawrence at No. 23. Dallas will also get a full season of Quinnen Williams after last year's midseason trade, and his 90.2 grade over the past three years makes him the clear top defender.

Free agency brought four more useful pieces in Rashan Gary, Dee Winters, Cobie Durant and Jalen Thompson, all 29 or younger with at least 650 snaps last season. Expect improvement ranging from modest to dramatic, with a slightly below-average unit the likeliest landing spot.

Kolar spent four years in Baltimore as mostly a blocker, but he graded 10th among tight ends in receiving and sixth in yards per route run over the last two seasons on very limited volume.

The Chargers paid him three years and $24.3 million, and through two preseason games he has worked as the primary receiving option ahead of David Njoku and Oronde Gadsden.

The open question is whether Gadsden takes the obvious passing downs, which we may not learn until after Week 1. He is a worthwhile late-round pick for anyone who already has a safer TE1, with top-12 upside if Gadsden stays buried.

Kamara was a perennial top-10 fantasy back on the strength of elite dual-threat grades, but his receiving efficiency has cratered since 2021, and he set career lows in both rushing and receiving grade in 2025 under Kellen Moore, whose offenses have historically suppressed running back value.

New Orleans signed Travis Etienne to lead the backfield, which leaves Kamara as a receiving back and a top backup.

We should expect much less fantasy production compared to recent seasons. His value is primarily as a flex option in very deep leagues and as a handcuff.

The Bears were an above-average fantasy defense last season, overcoming below-average points allowed with a league-leading 23 interceptions.

The unit will look very different in 2026 after losing four players with more than 950 snaps, including Tremaine Edmunds, Jaquan Brisker and Kevin Byard III, though Chicago replaced them well with Devin Bush, Coby Bryant and first-round safety Dillon Thieneman.

The health of cornerbacks Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon, both of whom missed time last season, will go a long way toward determining the ceiling. Treat Chicago as a matchup-based start, with a genuinely wide range of outcomes on either side.

Lane is a 6-foot-4 rookie with the hands and toughness to win contested catches and goal-line targets, and he appears to have won Baltimore's competition for the third receiver job. Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman sit ahead of him, but Bateman has graded at 62.

0 or lower in three of the last four seasons, which leaves a realistic path upward. Bateman is in a legal situation, which could also impact Lane's ability to surpass Bateman on the depth chart.

Catching passes from Lamar Jackson raises the ceiling if that happens. He is worth a late-round pick as a player who probably won't be startable but has a genuinely valuable outcome if he passes Bateman.

The Raiders allowed the eighth-most points last season but ranked third-worst in fantasy because they generated so few big plays.

Las Vegas lost linebackers Devin White, Elandon Roberts and Jamal Adams to free agency along with Kyu Blu Kelly and Tyree Wilson, then spent heavily to rebuild the front seven with Nakobe Dean, Quay Walker, Kwity Paye and Taron Johnson before adding five more defenders in the first five rounds of the draft.

The money was real, but the grades are not: Dean leads the group at 72.9 over the past three seasons, and none of the additions profile as difference-makers. The unit should be modestly better, without the kind of immediate leap other bottom-tier defenses might make.

Tampa Bay's defense graded around league average across the board last season, and more of the same looks likely in 2026. Cornerback Jamel Dean and his 80.

7 overall PFF grade left for Pittsburgh, with the two cornerbacks Tampa Bay drafted on Day 2 a year ago now expected to fill that void. Meanwhile, longtime linebacker Lavonte David retired, and three front-four rotation pieces departed.

The Buccaneers restocked up front with veterans and first-round edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr., which should mean an improved front seven paired with a step back in the secondary.

The Chargers ranked 14th among fantasy defenses last season, but they played better than that finish suggests.

Los Angeles’ zero defensive touchdowns and league-low fumble recoveries should regress in its favor.

With 10 of 11 starters back, the Chargers should be worth starting more weeks than not.

No defense allowed more yards than the Commanders last season at 6,533, and they ranked among the bottom six in points allowed and fantasy points. Six players with at least 200 snaps are now free agents, all of them 30 or older, including future Hall of Famers Bobby Wagner and Von Miller.

The headline addition is seventh overall pick Sonny Styles, with free agency bringing high-snap but low-graded players in Nick Cross, Amik Robertson and K'Lavon Chaisson, plus better-graded part-timers in Leo Chenal and Tim Settle.

The youth movement should pay off eventually, but it isn't likely to show up in the standings this season, so avoid Washington unless it outperforms expectations.

The Titans allowed the fifth-most points in the league last season at 478, and their slightly better fantasy finish leaned on four defensive and special teams touchdowns.

The roster has been depleted since, with only seven of the 17 players who logged at least 300 snaps still around, and just Jeffery Simmons and Cedric Gray clearing 400 snaps with a grade above 55.0. Tennessee brought in eight defenders with at least 400 snaps last season, most grading between 61.

0 and 66.0. The headline moves were hiring head coach Robert Saleh as well as drafting Keldric Faulk 31st overall and Anthony Hill Jr. in the second round. This will take time to come together, so leave the Titans on the waiver wire.

Fields is a 6-foot-4, 222-pound X receiver taken 74th overall with excellent hands, blocking and toughness that fit a John Harbaugh offense. However, his college receiving grades were good rather than great, and he profiled better against zone than man.

He lands in a crowded New York room behind Malik Nabers, Darius Slayton and a wave of free-agent additions. In the second preseason game, Fields only played on the first drive.

The one remaining challenger for playing time is Mooney. Fields is a fine late round dart throw, as he has the most upside for any wide receiver on the Giants other than Nabers.

Dotson has spent two seasons as an afterthought in Philadelphia, drawing targets on 7.8% of his routes, the lowest rate among 132 qualifying receivers.

Atlanta signed him to a two-year deal, and he has worked as the clear No. 2 behind Drake London throughout camp and the preseason, but Kyle Pitts and Bijan Robinson still sit ahead of him in the target order.

He is a late-round dart throw in deeper leagues, valuable mainly as insurance if one of those three miss time.

Robinson was a productive early-down lead back in Washington but saw his role collapse after a preseason trade to San Francisco, where he sat behind an healthy Christian McCaffrey.

He signs with Atlanta as the clear backup to Bijan Robinson under new coach Kevin Stefanski, whose scheme has historically favored an early-down runner, though Bijan Robinson is locked in for passing-down work.

His standalone value is limited unless the offense overperforms, and the biggest question is how goal-line carries get split. His real appeal is handcuff value, since he'd likely inherit a starter's workload if Bijan Robinson missed time.

The Vikings ranked fifth among fantasy defenses last season, though regression is coming after they led the league with 13 fumble recoveries and added two defensive touchdowns.

Minnesota lost four players with more than 500 snaps, including Jonathan Allen, Javon Hargrave, Jonathan Greenard and longtime safety Harrison Smith, while James Pierre was the only notable free-agent addition.

The Vikings instead rebuilt through the draft, taking four defenders in the first two days, led by first-rounder Caleb Banks. That should pay off long term, but a slow start is possible while the rookies get up to speed.

Waller was a top-three fantasy tight end in 2019 and 2020, and even through the injuries that followed he has kept producing at a high level whenever he is on the field, grading out second among tight ends in receiving last season.

The problem is that he is rarely on the field. He has missed at least five games in five straight seasons and turns 34 before Week 1.

He signed with the Carolina Panthers during training camp to take the receiving tight end role, and while the offense around him is unlikely to be good, that has never stopped him before. He is a late-round dart throw who cannot be trusted as a season-long starter but should deliver usable weeks.

The Saints ranked 12th in fantasy points last season, helped by three defensive touchdowns and 10 fumble recoveries, which tied for fourth-most, though they were only average in points allowed against one of the league's easiest schedules.

New Orleans then lost linebacker Demario Davis and his 89.2 grade over the past three seasons, along with starting cornerback Alontae Taylor to Tennessee. Kaden Elliss returns from Atlanta to take over for Davis, and his 75.

4 three-year grade is solid without matching what Davis provided, while the 2025 mid-round picks will be counted on at cornerback. Some regression is coming regardless of the roster, and these changes tilt New Orleans toward a step back.

Noel outgraded Christian Kirk on a per-route basis as a rookie despite a smaller role, and Kirk's departure opens the door for Noel to take over the slot. The problem is that the path to playing time remains difficult.

Ideally, Noel would have spent training camp also playing Z in two wide receiver sets, but injuries prevented him from participation in most of training camp. Houston added tight ends which point toward more two-tight-end sets that would shrink Noel’s snaps further.

That combination caps his floor and his ceiling unless he seizes the clear No. 2 role. He is an okay deeper-league target as a talented young receiver in a strong offense.

The Falcons finished as the 11th-best fantasy defense last season on the strength of big plays, ranking second with 57 sacks and sixth with 16 interceptions despite sitting below-average in points allowed.

Atlanta lost two front-seven contributors in Kaden Elliss and David Onyemata, both of whom graded above 75.0 over the past three seasons, and none of the replacements brought in exceeded 500 snaps or a 70.

0 grade last season. Edge rusher James Pearce Jr. was suspended for thalf the season while Jalon Walker is out for the year with a torn ACL, moving Atlanta from a likely weekly start to a situational one.

While the defense might be better, the schedule is more difficult.

The Panthers have the sixth-worst schedule for defenses, according to our strength of schedule tool.

There might only be a few weeks where it makes sense to put Carolina in a fantasy starting lineup in a standard 12-team league, even if the Panthers finish among the top 20 most weeks.

Douglas carved out the Patriots' slot role as a rookie and grew into a 66-target season in 2024 before Stefon Diggs and a heavy dose of 12 personnel cut his snap rate to 26.

3% in 2025. The talent never went anywhere, as his PFF receiving grade hit a career high and his 1.64 yards per route run over the last three seasons ranks 38th among wide receivers.

New England has since cleared out Diggs and Kayshon Boutte, and camp reports have Douglas on the field whenever the offense is in 11 personnel, with Josh McDaniels calling the plays. He is still tied to a single personnel grouping, but he is worth a late-round pick in deeper leagues.

Bateman has been the Ravens' X receiver for five seasons but has never turned the role into fantasy production, ranking near the bottom of the league in both target rate and yards per route run last season.

Baltimore keeps adding receivers who can play his position, including two more in the 2026 draft. Bateman is facing a legal situation which could result in him missing some time this season.

The case for Bateman is thin but real: A new coaching staff, a starting job alongside an MVP quarterback and a nine-touchdown season on his resume from 2024. He is a deeper-league option only, with an outside chance at flex value.

Bernard is a versatile, well-rounded receiver with no glaring weaknesses but no elite trait either, and he landed in Pittsburgh behind D.K.

Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. He will battle Roman Wilson for the third receiver job, and recent history suggests Day 2 rookies do not always seize those roles immediately.

Even if Bernard wins it, the volume likely will not be there for fantasy without an injury ahead of him. He is a speculative late-round pick in deep leagues with more appeal in dynasty, given the uncertainty around both veterans' futures in Pittsburgh.

Bigsby carved out a legitimate role in Philadelphia last season after losing his job in Jacksonville, flashing with a 104-yard game in Week 8 and 16-to-17-carry outings late in the year on the way to becoming Saquon Barkley's primary backup.

His efficiency numbers were notably better than Barkley's, with a higher rushing grade and more yards after contact, which could mean a bigger workload this season, though that mainly matters in very deep leagues.

He's the clear handcuff to Barkley, but his almost nonexistent receiving production (11 catches in 50 career games) means a Barkley injury wouldn't be a clean hand-down, since Will Shipley would likely absorb passing-game work, making Bigsby a lesser standalone option than his per-touch efficiency suggests.

Miami ranked below-average in every major defensive metric last season without ever bottoming out. The roster has since been gutted, particularly in the secondary, where all five of the Dolphins’ top defensive backs by snap count are gone.

The replacements are thin, with former Titans cornerback Darrell Baker Jr. the only free-agent addition who started last season and everyone else compiling 350 snaps or fewer, though first-round cornerback Chris Johnson should start right away.

New head coach Jeff Hafley, a longtime defensive backs coach, is the primary reason for optimism, but that improvement will take time. Avoid the Dolphins early in the season.

Arizona ranked among the bottom six in points allowed, yards allowed and fantasy points last season, without a single player clearing 600 snaps and a 70.0 grade.

Unlike most bottom-tier defenses, the Cardinals neither spent big in free agency nor invested draft capital, losing Calais Campbell, Dalvin Tomlinson, Akeem Davis-Gaither and Jalen Thompson while adding only Andrew Wingard, Jack Gibbens and Andrew Billings, none of whom graded above 64.

0. Just two of their draft picks went to defense, both on Day 3, and defensive coordinator Nick Rallis was retained despite the head coaching change. There is little here to suggest improvement, so Arizona is a defense to avoid.

Harris spent four healthy seasons as Pittsburgh's lead back, finishing around RB20 annually on volume rather than efficiency, before a torn Achilles cut short his one year with the Los Angeles Chargers.

He signed with the New York Giants in the middle of training camp, reuniting with the coaching staff that faced him twice a year in Baltimore and fitting the big-back profile John Harbaugh has always favored.

He joins a crowded backfield led by Cam Skattebo, but his size should earn him rotational and goal-line work, and he has a real path to the lead role if Skattebo's own injury recovery stalls. He is a handcuff with modest upside but a better-than-usual chance at standalone flex value.

Mooney has been a steady starter but rarely a fantasy factor across six NFL seasons, and his modest one-year deal with the Giants drops him into a crowded receiver room behind Malik Nabers, with Darius Slayton, Malachi Fields and Odell Beckham Jr. likely fighting for outside snaps.

Mooney’s best path to playing time is the slot, where his familiarity with new coordinator Matt Nagy from their Chicago years and relatively light competition there make him the favorite.

That alone likely isn't enough for fantasy relevance, but Nabers' ACL and meniscus recovery is the wild-card: If Nabers isn't ready for Week 1, Mooney could briefly become the offense's top receiving weapon. He's a sensible late-round dart, especially for managers banking on rookies or other receivers who could start slowly.

Allen bounced through four college seasons across three schools before a move to the slot at Cincinnati produced 12 touchdowns and a 2.42 yards per route run mark, which the Kansas City Chiefs bought into with a fifth-round pick.

Injuries to Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy have handed him extensive first-team work all summer, and he has drawn steady praise along with apparent trust from Patrick Mahomes.

He should open the season fourth on the depth chart with real snaps but not enough volume to start in fantasy. He is a late-round flier whose payoff, if it comes, is likelier to arrive in the back half of the season than the front.

TeSlaa flashed late as a rookie, catching 12 passes with four touchdowns over his final six games once injuries opened up playing time. He moves up to third on the depth chart with Kalif Raymond gone, but the target competition in Detroit is brutal, with Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams, Jahmyr Gibbs and Sam LaPorta all ahead of him.

His calling card is scoring, converting six of 16 career catches into touchdowns thanks to a size advantage over Detroit's other pass-catchers. He is a spike-week option whose real value would come if a Lions receiver were to miss extended time.

Reviews in training camp have been mixed, and he played with the backups during the first two preseason games, suggesting his job as the third wide receiver might not be secure.

Wicks was a talented but flawed depth piece in Green Bay, grading as the worst of a deep receiver room while registering elite tackle-avoidance alongside too many drops and fumbles.

A trade to Philadelphia gives him a clearer path: With A.J. Brown and Jahan Dotson gone, he projects as the Eagles' X receiver opposite DeVonta Smith next to rookie Makai Lemon in the slot.

Smith is the clear top target and Lemon could emerge as the second option, but if the rookie is limited to three-receiver sets, Wicks' every-down role gives him a route to relevance. In a good Eagles offense that has supported two fantasy receivers, he is worth a late-round pick in deeper leagues.

Bryant carved out a steady slot role as a rookie, playing half the snaps from Week 5 on, though he cleared 50 yards only once and scored just one touchdown.

The Broncos then traded a first-round pick for Jaylen Waddle, which caps the upside for everyone behind him, and Bryant projects as the third receiver in three-wide sets.

His real path is at X, where Courtland Sutton‘s contract could become expendable after this season and where the two graded closer than the depth chart suggests. He is a late-round dart throw whose usage is worth tracking week to week.

Dell looked like a legitimate fantasy starter as a rookie in 2023 before a quiet second season ended with a knee injury severe enough to cost him all of 2025 as well.

He is easing back into practice now, and Jayden Higgins‘ season-ending ACL injury cleared much of the traffic that had been blocking his path to snaps.

Xavier Hutchinson is the favorite to open the season in that role, but the job is winnable if Dell's health cooperates. He is worth a late-round pick as a patience play, with most of his value likely arriving in the second half of the season.

Perine has spent most of his career as a third-down specialist, including an earlier Cincinnati stint from 2020 to 2022 behind Joe Mixon, with stops in Denver and Kansas City before returning in 2025. He saw more early-down work as last season progressed, partly because of early struggles from Chase Brown, including two 14-carry games against the Baltimore Ravens.

He is unlikely to hold standalone value unless the Bengals are blowing teams out, but he would probably lead the backfield if Brown were to get hurt, with only 2025 sixth-round pick Tahj Brooks behind him.

That handcuff appeal, in a quality offense where the staff clearly trusts him, makes Perine a late-round option in deeper leagues where most backup running backs are rostered.

A well-balanced slot receiver who can also handle the Z, Cooper was the second pass catcher the Jets took on the opening day of the 2026 draft. The fit is awkward, though, as Garrett Wilson occupies the same Z/slot territory and Adonai Mitchell is the clear X, leaving the rookie to compete for three-receiver-set snaps.

Cooper was a backup in the first preseason game, but took over as the primary slot receiver in 11 personnel in the second game. Cooper will likely need significant snaps in two wide receiver sets to reach fantasy value.

Luckily, he took snaps for Adonai Mitchell with the starters, and continued to take snaps as an outside receiver with the backups. He is a fine late round target.

Lloyd has been a ghost through two NFL seasons, with hamstring, ankle and appendicitis issues limiting him to a small role in a single regular-season game.

Green Bay still appears to view him as the primary backup behind Josh Jacobs, with the depth chart thin enough that no one is clearly ahead of him. That matters because Jacobs is a proven top-10 back, and an injury or suspension would hand Lloyd a genuinely valuable role.

The injury risk is obvious and the Packers could always add competition, making him a late-round target, as long as the Packers don't add to their running back room.

Allgeier was strong early as a rookie but was stuck behind Bijan Robinson, settling into a short-yardage role that lowered his yards per carry while keeping his success rate strong.

He signed with Arizona hoping to lead the backfield, only for the Cardinals to draft Jeremiyah Love, and a worse offensive line makes it a tougher spot than Atlanta. The one bit of hope is that the split is unsettled, and early-round backs don't always dominate immediately, as David Montgomery showed alongside Jahmyr Gibbs in Detroit.

Love has a high ankle sprain, increasing the chances Allgeier is a factor early in the season. Allgeier is a deeper-league flex option, but in smaller leagues, there are better-situated handcuffs to target.

Hurst is a contested-catch X receiver who was picked by Tampa Bay in the third round. While a room that includes Emeka Egbuka, Chris Godwin and Jalen McMillan looks crowded, coordinator Zac Robinson has hinted at an alignment shuffle that would open the X spot for Hurst.

Robinson compared him to Odell Beckham Jr. in the Rams' Super Bowl season, a lane that produced seven touchdowns in 12 games despite inconsistent yardage.

With Mike Evans gone, there is a path to Hurst inheriting the contested end-zone targets that made Evans a touchdown machine. He is not typically the kind of rookie worth drafting, but continued camp buzz would make him a late-round sleeper.

Allen is buried in a three-back committee behind Breece Hall, with his role further squeezed by Isaiah Davis, and an MCL sprain ended his 2025 after just three-plus games.

Head coach Aaron Glenn still plans a three-headed rotation, so his snap share projects around 25-30% again. The path to standalone value runs through his size, since at a reported 250 pounds he profiles as the goal-line back and could produce if the offense overachieves.

Failing that, his main value is as the primary handcuff to Hall, who is currently dealing with a groin strain, and has a chance of missing Week 1.

Washington is a rare 6-foot-2, 228-pound power back who lands in Las Vegas with a clear path to the No. 2 job behind Ashton Jeanty, since both primary backups from last season are gone.

His size gives him a plausible claim to goal-line work, the kind of role that carries real touchdown value even in a limited snap share. He also profiles as Jeanty's handcuff. Jeanty suffered an ankle sprain on Aug. 23.

It's unclear if Jeanty will be ready to go for Week 1 or if he will miss some time. Washington could quickly move up draft boards if it becomes known that Jeanty will miss some time, as Washington would be a top-24 option at running back for as long as Jeanty is out.

An undrafted free agent in 2024, he spent his first two seasons on special teams and as a third-string back before Zach Charbonnet's playoff ACL tear pushed him into the second running back role for the conference championship game and Super Bowl, where he handled third downs and two-minute work.

Kenneth Walker III is now gone and Charbonnet is still recovering, leaving first-round rookie Jadarian Price as the primary competition, with Price expected to handle early downs and Holani third downs until Charbonnet returns.

Winning the goal-line carries or beating out Price in camp would put him in flex range. He is unlikely to matter for long, but he is the cheapest back you can draft and plausibly start in Week 1.

Sanders went from a projected top pick to a fifth-round selection in the 2025 NFL Draft and averaged 13.2 fantasy points per game over his final seven starts, hampered by both low passing volume and a league-worst 45.5 offensive grade among quarterbacks with at least 300 snaps.

Cleveland has since invested heavily in the offense, drafting wide receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston in the first two rounds while rebuilding the offensive line, and the trade of Myles Garrett could force the Browns into more pass-heavy game scripts.

If Sanders wins the starting job, there is a path to QB2 value in superflex leagues. The challenge is that he is competing with Deshaun Watson, and with two first-round picks in next year's draft, Cleveland remains well positioned to select another quarterback, leaving no one's hold on the job particularly secure.

Wright spent his rookie year buried in a crowded Miami backfield before taking over as the primary backup midway through last season, with a 107-yard game in Week 14 as the highlight.

He appears to have held that job into this year, playing as the clear second back in the first two preseason games while Ollie Gordon II worked deeper into the game with the reserves.

He has little standalone value behind De'Von Achane, and the offense around him limits his appeal relative to other handcuffs, but he would step into a top-30 role immediately if Achane went down.

Tracy has started 23 of 34 possible games over his first two seasons, an impressive feat for a former fifth-round pick. His fantasy production, however, has been heavily dependent on volume and touchdowns, while his efficiency grades rank near the bottom among running backs with at least 250 carries.

He had already lost the starting job to Cam Skattebo before Skattebo’s season-ending injury, and Skattebo appears on track for Week 1 after starting the Giants’ preseason opener. Tracy’s outlook became even murkier with the addition of Najee Harris, putting him at risk of falling further down the depth chart.

Tracy could carve out a role on passing downs, though New York could prefer another back in pass protection. At this point, a trade to a running back-needy team might offer Tracy his best path to renewed fantasy relevance.

Stowers brings rare athleticism and receiving production to the position, earning a 91.4 career PFF receiving grade at Vanderbilt that surpasses several recent first-round tight ends. He also tested in the 95th percentile in multiple combine drills. His sub-240-pound frame is the primary concern, though recent undersized tight ends such as Harold Fannin Jr. have shown that smaller players can still thrive at the position.

Stowers will begin his career behind Dallas Goedert, but with Goedert turning 32 and playing on a reduced contract, the rookie looks like a potential successor in 2027 and beyond. Philadelphia has produced a top-12 fantasy tight end in seven consecutive seasons, making the long-term opportunity particularly appealing. The immediate outlook is less exciting.

Stowers could rank third among Philadelphia's tight ends in snaps as a rookie, with blocking-oriented options potentially playing ahead of him. Barring a Goedert injury or a standout training camp, Stowers is unlikely to make a significant fantasy impact in 2026, but he profiles as one of the better tight end handcuffs in deeper leagues.

Coleman is an unusual back, short and thick at 5-foot-8 and 228 pounds, with excellent contact balance plus receiving and pass-protection ability. He joined a deep Denver room, where J.K.

Dobbins, RJ Harvey, Tyler Badie and Jaleel McLaughlin all return, and the likeliest outcome is a three-man committee with an unpredictable snap split. He was the third back based on the first preseason game.

Coleman’s pass-protection skill gives him a plausible path to third-down work, and Dobbins' injury history leaves a route to a bigger role. But Sean Payton's history with backs like Mark Ingram suggests a slow build, making Coleman a late-round deep-league pick rather than a 2026 contributor.

Black has the athletic profile of a three-down back, with above-average speed, acceleration and change of direction for this class, and his zone-heavy running style is a clean fit for Kyle Shanahan's scheme.

The concerns are a lack of receiving production and some hesitation identifying lanes in power concepts. He was the only back taken on Day 2 and has a serious chance to win the backup job over Jordan James and Isaac Guerendo.

All three have dealt with injuries during training camp, but only Black was healthy enough for their second preseason game. Given McCaffrey's injury history, whoever wins that job carries standalone value, making Black a late-round sleeper.

Davis is locked into a three-man Buffalo backfield behind James Cook, and his usage actually shrank in 2025, with seven games without a carry and nearly half his season rushing total coming in a Week 18 blowout.

He should see more work this season, but not enough to start in most leagues. His real value is as Cook's handcuff, and the flashes are there, including a 20-carry, 97-yard game plus 55 receiving yards when Cook missed Week 6 as a rookie.

If Cook were to miss time, Davis would likely lead the backfield in one of the league's best offenses, making him a must-start and one of the more appealing pure handcuffs in fantasy.

Tolbert never locked down a consistent role in Dallas, peaking in 2024 before falling behind on the depth chart in 2025, and a move to Miami gives him a genuine opening.

The Dolphins gutted their receiver room, moving on from Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle and leaving Malik Washington as the only notable holdover, so Tolbert steps into a wide-open competition among six receivers.

Through the first two preseason games, he appears to be competing with Jalen Reagor for the third spot on the depth chart. Tolbert should remain off fantasy rosters until he can re-gain a full time role.

Gadsden flashed as a rookie, leading all tight ends in fantasy points during a Weeks 6-9 tear before hitting a rookie wall. His 2026 setup is mixed: new coordinator Mike McDaniel runs a faster, more pass-heavy scheme that fits his athletic profile, but the Chargers added Charlie Kolar and David Njoku, crowding the position and threatening his snaps.

Both were among the starters who rested during the first week of the preseason, while Gadsden played with the backups, confirming Kolar and Njoku will have significant roles.

There's still a breakout path if he settles into the receiving role while the others handle blocking and hybrid duties, though the playing time is a genuine question. He's an intriguing dynasty target for the patient and only a late-round pick in redraft.

James spent his rookie year buried on the depth chart, sitting as a healthy inactive for 15 weeks before earning a special teams role late, with his only offensive touches coming in a playoff blowout.

Brian Robinson Jr. is gone, but San Francisco drafted Kaelon Black in the third round, leaving James in a direct camp battle for the backup job behind Christian McCaffrey. That job matters, since McCaffrey has missed significant time in three of the past five seasons.

James has missed most of training camp with fractured ribs, which has made it difficult for him to win the backup job. He is no longer a late round pick, as we are unlikely to know where he sits relative to Black until after WEek 1.

Joe Milton, a 2024 sixth-round pick of the New England Patriots, served as a rookie third-stringer before playing nearly every snap in Week 18 against the Buffalo Bills, where his 95.

8 offensive grade was the third-best by a quarterback in any game that season. Dallas traded for him to be the primary backup, and he attempted 24 passes over four games, most of them in that Week 18 finale.

The Cowboys then traded for Sam Howell to compete with Joe Milton for the backup job, but if Milton wins it, he is one of the better backup options given Dallas' willingness to throw and the talent around him.

Blue was a fifth-round pick by Dallas in 2025 and a common sleeper, since many thought he could win the starting job ahead of Javonte Williams and Miles Sanders, but he opened the year behind both and was often a healthy inactive on a roster that usually kept only three active backs plus fullback Hunter Luepke.

A Sanders injury gave him limited run from Weeks 5 to 8, where he managed 22 carries for 65 yards and a catch before losing the backup job to Malik Davis, though he flashed in Week 18 with 16 carries for 64 yards and a touchdown.

Brian Schottenheimer has praised his second-year approach as “night and day,” and Dallas seems to want Blue to win the backup job over Davis and Phil Mafah. While Blue started the first presesaon game, he played behind Davis in the second game. He should be avoided unless he can earn the backup running back job.

Allen, a sixth-round pick with a punishing, tackle-breaking style but limited receiving and speed, profiles as a likely short-yardage and goal-line piece in a busy Washington backfield that also includes Jacory Croskey-Merritt, Rachaad White and Jeremy McNichols.

Allen has generated unusually strong buzz from coaches and beat writers during OTAs, but that has slowed during training camp. He will need to show he can take some playing time from Croskey-Merritt before being drafted in most leagues.

Even in the best case, sharing the backfield with White as the third-down back caps Allen as a low-end fantasy starter, making him a name worth drafting only if the training camp hype holds up.

Williams is a polished slot receiver out of Clemson whose profile, a smaller frame and 11-personnel-only usage among comparable players, typically caps fantasy ceiling, though Zay Flowers and Jaylen Waddle show that outcome isn't universal.

He is competing for Washington's slot job over Jaylin Lane and Luke McCaffrey. He is currently behind them based on preseason usage. The Commanders wide receiver room now has two established starters in Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs.

The Diggs signing cost Williams his late-round sleeper appeal, leaving his path tied to passing several players on the depth chart and an injury to one of the two veterans, both of whom are in their 30s.

Singletary spent four years with the Buffalo Bills, one with the Houston Texans, and the last two with the New York Giants. In New York, he has been a role player, eventually losing his starting job to Tyrone Tracy Jr., and then falling to third on the depth chart when Cam Skattebo.

He was part of a three man rotation with the starters in their first preseason game, suggesting he would see more playing time than a typical third back. New York signed Najee Harris, which further complicated the running back rotation.

Singletary played ahead of Tracy in the second preseason game. Considering Singletary is currently ahead of Tracy, and both Skattebo and Harris missed the end of last season due to injury, it’s entirely possible there are weeks where Singeltary is New York’s lead running back this season.

Conner has been one of the more productive backs in football when healthy, posting his two best seasons at ages 28 and 29 and finishing top-13 in fantasy points per game in four straight years with Arizona.

A foot and ankle injury limited him to three games in 2025, and the Cardinals responded by adding Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier ahead of him. He now has no clear route to touches in Arizona unless Love's high ankle sprain continues to bother him, and Allgeier also suffers an injury.

He may not even survive roster cuts, so his fantasy case rests almost entirely on landing somewhere else. That makes him a smart flier in leagues that force you to start a kicker or defense without forcing you to draft one, since you can hold him through camp and cut him if nothing changes.

Claiborne is an undersized, change-of-direction rookie who profiles as a pass-catching specialist in the mold of Justice Hill, a role that has produced fantasy value for players like Kenneth Gainwell.

He landed in Minnesota behind Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason, with Jones as his more direct competition for receiving work. However, Jones' age, recent injury history and declining efficiency open a path for Claiborne to take over that role at some point this season.

Even then, Claiborne would likely only absorb part of Jones' workload rather than inherit it outright, capping his redraft value. A strong rookie season could set him up for a bigger role in 2027, when neither Jones nor Mason is under contract. He's a fine dynasty stash, best drafted only in deep redraft leagues.
